The statutory basis is \nprepared in accordance with the Corporations Act 2001 (Cth) and the Australian Accounting Standards, which comply with \nInternational Financial Reporting Standards (IFRS). The cash basis is used by management to present a clear view of the \nBank\u2019s operating results. It is not a measure based on cash accounting or cash flows. The items excluded from cash profit, such \nas hedging and IFRS volatility and losses or gains on acquisition, disposal, closure, capital repatriation and demerger of \nbusinesses are calculated consistently with the prior year and prior half disclosures and do not discriminate between positive \nand negative adjustments. A list of items excluded from cash profit is provided on page 3 of the Group\u2019s 31 December 2025 PA, \nwhich can be accessed at our website: www.commbank.com.au/results\nLevel 1\nCBA parent bank, offshore branches and extended licensed entities approved by APRA. \nLevel 2\nConsolidated banking group including banking subsidiaries such as ASB Bank and CBA Europe N.V.\nCorporate \nTroublesome\nCorporate Troublesome includes exposures to corporate customers where profitability is weak and the capacity to meet \nfinancial commitments is diminished. These customers are at higher risk of default over the next 12 months.\nCredit Valuation \nAdjustment (CVA)\nThe market value of the counterparty credit risk on the derivative portfolio, calculated as the difference between the risk-free \nportfolio value and the portfolio value that takes into account the possibility of a counterparty\u2019s default.\nDerivative \nValuation \nAdjustments (XVA)\nA number of different valuation adjustments are made to the value of derivative contracts to reflect the additional costs or \nbenefits in holding these contracts. The material valuation adjustments included within the CBA result are CVA and FVA. \nFunding Valuation \nAdjustment (FVA)\nThe expected funding cost or benefit over the life of the uncollateralised derivative portfolio.\nHigh Quality Liquid \nAssets (HQLA)\nAs defined by APRA in Australian Prudential Standard APS210 Liquidity. Qualifying HQLA includes cash, government and \nsemi-government securities, and RBNZ eligible securities. \nInternational \nCapital\nThe measure is based on the Australian Banking Association publication \u2018Basel 3.1 Capital Comparison Study\u2019 (March 2023), \nwhich compares APRA\u2019s capital framework, including RBNZ prudential requirements, with the finalised post-crisis Basel III \nreforms. \nLeverage Ratio\nTier 1 Capital divided by Total exposures, expressed as a percentage. Total exposures are the sum of On Balance Sheet items, \nderivatives, Securities Financing Transactions (SFTs), and Off Balance Sheet items, net of any Tier 1 regulatory deductions that \nare already included in these items.\nLiquidity Coverage \nRatio (LCR)\nThe LCR is the first quantitative liquidity measure that is part of the Basel III reforms. It was implemented by APRA in Australia \non 1 January 2015. It requires Australian ADIs to hold sufficient liquid assets to meet 30 day net cash outflows projected under \nan APRA-prescribed stress scenario.\nMain Financial \nInstitution (MFI) \nshare \u2013 Retail\nMFI share measures the proportion of Banking and Finance MFI Customers that nominated each bank as their MFI. MFI \ndefinition: In the Roy Morgan Single Source Survey MFI is a customer determined response where one institution is nominated \nas the primary financial institution they deal with (when considering all financial products they hold). Peers include ANZ Group \n(including Suncorp from August 2024), NAB Group and Westpac Group (including St George Group). CBA Group includes \nBankwest. Source: Roy Morgan Single Source survey conducted by Roy Morgan, Australian population 14+ (12 month \naverages to December 2025), excl. unable to identify MFI. Roy Morgan has re-calibrated the results from April 2020 to March \n2021 to take into account methodology changes since COVID-19. This has resulted in small differences to some of the \npreviously published figures. \nMFI Share \u2013 \nBusiness\nRFI Global Atlas Business MFI Share. Data on a 6 month roll weighted to the Australian business population. MFI Customer \nShare is the proportion of all businesses with any business banking, that nominate the FI as their main financial institution. \nShare based on grouped brands as follows: CBA Group includes CBA and Bankwest, ANZ Group includes ANZ and Suncorp \nfrom August 2024, NAB Group includes NAB, Westpac Group includes Westpac, St George, BankSA and Bank of Melbourne.\nMFI Share \u2013 \nInstitutional\nRFI Global Atlas Business Institutional MFI Share. Data on a 12 month roll weighted to the Australian business population with \nan annual revenue of $500 million or more for the previous financial year. MFI Customer Share is the proportion of all \nbusinesses with any business banking, that nominate the FI as their main financial institution. Share based on grouped brands \nas follows: CBA Group includes CBA and Bankwest, ANZ Group includes ANZ and Suncorp from August 2024, NAB Group \nincludes NAB, Westpac Group includes Westpac, St George, BankSA and Bank of Melbourne.\nTerm\nDescription\nNPS \u2013 Consumer\nRFI Global Atlas Consumer MFI NPS. Based on Australian population aged 14+ years old rating their likelihood to recommend \ntheir MFI. NPS results are shown as a six-month rolling average. NPS is reported for each brand, therefore Commonwealth Bank \nof Australia excludes Bankwest and ASB Banking Group.\nNPS \u2013 Business \nRFI Global Atlas Business MFI NPS. Based on Australian businesses rating their likelihood to recommend their MFI for Business \nBanking. NPS results are shown as a six-month rolling average. NPS is reported for each brand, therefore Commonwealth Bank of \nAustralia excludes Bankwest and ASB Banking Group.\nNPS \u2013 Institutional RFI Global Atlas Institutional $300 million plus Business MFI NPS: Based on Australian businesses with an annual revenue of \n$300 million or more for the previous financial year rating their likelihood to recommend their MFI for Business Banking. NPS \nresults are shown as a 12 month rolling average. NPS is reported for each brand, therefore Commonwealth Bank of Australia \nexcludes Bankwest and ASB Banking Group.\nNPS \u2013 Consumer \nMobile App \nRFI Global Atlas Consumer MFI Mobile Banking App NPS: Based on MFI customers rating their likelihood to recommend their \nMFI\u2019s Mobile Banking App used in the last 4 weeks. NPS results are shown as a six-month rolling average. NPS is reported for \neach brand, therefore Commonwealth Bank of Australia excludes Bankwest and ASB Banking Group.\nNPS \u2013 Consumer \nDigital Banking\nRFI Global Atlas Consumer MFI Digital Banking NPS: Based on MFI customers rating their likelihood to recommend their MFI\u2019s \nMobile Banking App and/or Online Banking used in the last four weeks. Overall Digital NPS is then calculated by weighting Online \nBanking: Mobile Banking App by a factor of 23.8:76.2. NPS results are shown as a six-month rolling average. NPS is reported for \neach brand, therefore Commonwealth Bank of Australia excludes Bankwest and ASB Banking Group.\nNPS \u2013 Business \nDigital Banking\nRFI Global Atlas Business MFI Digital Banking NPS: Based on MFI customers (turnover below $40m) rating their likelihood to \nrecommend their MFI\u2019s Mobile Banking App and/or Online Banking used in the last 4 weeks. Overall Digital NPS is then calculated \nby weighting Online Banking: Mobile Banking App by a factor of 41:59. NPS results are shown as a six-month rolling average. \nNPS is reported for each brand, therefore Commonwealth Bank of Australia excludes Bankwest and ASB Banking Group.\nNPS & Share \nRanks\nNPS and MFI Share ranks are based on absolute scores, or simple comparisons of incidences among major banks, not statistically \nsignificant differences. \nNet Stable \nFunding Ratio \n(NSFR)\nThe NSFR is the second quantitative liquidity measure of the Basel III reforms, in addition to the LCR. It was implemented by \nAPRA in Australia on 1 January 2018. It requires Australian ADIs to fund their assets with sufficient stable funding to reduce \nfunding risk over a one year horizon. APRA prescribed factors are used to determine the stable funding requirement of assets and \nthe stability of funding.\nNon-Performing \nExposures\nAn exposure which is in default, meaning it is 90 days or more past-due or it is considered unlikely the borrower will repay the \nexposure in full without recourse to actions such as realising security.\nRepTrak \nreputation score\nRepTrak, The RepTrak Company. Data is collected throughout the quarter and reported at quarter end. The reputation score is a \ncalculation based on four statements measuring esteem, admiration and respect, trust and good feeling towards the organisation; \nexpressed as a score ranging from 0-100 to determine the reputational strength of the company.\nRisk Weighted \nAssets (RWA)\nThe value of the Group\u2019s On and Off Balance Sheet assets are adjusted by risk weights calculated according to various APRA \nprudential standards. For more information, refer to the APRA website.\nTotal Committed \nExposures (TCE)\nTotal Committed Exposures is defined as the balance outstanding and undrawn components of committed facility limits. \nIt is calculated post receipt of eligible financial collateral that meets the Group\u2019s netting requirements and excludes settlement \nexposures.\nTroublesome & \nNon-Performing \nExposures (TNPE)\nTroublesome and non-performing exposures (TNPE) have replaced the Group\u2019s previous Troublesome and Impaired assets \nmeasures to align with the industry standard measure of Non-Performing. TNPE comprises Non-Performing exposures and \nCorporate troublesome exposures.\n", "135\nDanny John\nMedia Relations \n+61 2 9595 3219 \nMedia@cba.com.au\nMelanie Kirk\nInvestor Relations\n+61 2 9118 7113\nCBAInvestorRelations@cba.com.au\nContact us\nInvestor Relations\nMedia Relations\n"]
data/cache/pages/CBA-FY26-asx-announcement.json:1:["Commonwealth Bank of Australia \n\u2502 ACN 123 123 124 \n\u2502 12 August 2026 \n\u2502 Media Release 215/2026\nCommonwealth Bank Place South, Level 1, 11 Harbour Street, Sydney NSW 2000\ni\nASX Announcement\nFY26 Results\nFor the year ended 30 June 2026\n1\nDisciplined franchise growth; \ninvesting for the future\nFor footnotes see page iv of this ASX Announcement\nResults overview\nCBA delivered a strong FY26 result. Cash net profit after tax increased \n7% to $11bn, pre-provision profit increased 6% to $16.5bn and return \non equity rose to 14.0%. Operating income increased 6%, supported \nby customer and volume growth and a broadly stable underlying net \ninterest margin. In FY26, CBA grew at or above system in each of our \nfive core domestic product categories: home lending, business \nlending, consumer finance, household deposits and business \ndeposits. It is the first time CBA has achieved this and the first time \nany major Australian bank has done so in the past 15 years. We \nremain the main financial institution for one in three Australians and \none in four Australian businesses.\nGrowth remained broad across home lending, business lending and \ncustomer deposits, supported by stronger transaction relationships. \nWe continued to invest in customer service, technology, operational \nresilience and productivity. Investment spend increased 6% to $2.4bn. \nThe franchise continued to grow through the second half despite \ncompetition. Loan impairment expense increased from low levels and \narrears rose in some consumer portfolios, while realised credit losses \nremained low, overall credit quality remained sound and provision \ncoverage remained strong.\nWe provided more than 147,000 tailored payment arrangements to \ncustomers needing support and encourage customers experiencing \ndifficulty to contact us early. We also invested more than $1bn during \nthe year to help protect customers from fraud, scams, cyber threats \nand financial crime.\n \nThe Board has determined a final dividend of $2.70 per share, fully \nfranked, taking our dividend for the full year to $5.05 per share.\nOutlook\nThe Australian economy has remained resilient, supported by \nhistorically low unemployment and longer-term investment. However \ngrowth is slowing, with higher interest rates and inflation placing \nuneven pressure on household incomes and economic activity. \nHousing activity has softened from a high base. Application volumes \nappear to have stabilised in recent weeks. Businesses continue to \nmanage higher input costs and supply uncertainty. CBA enters FY27 \nwith leading customer relationships, a broader franchise and a strong \nbalance sheet. Our priorities are to deepen primary customer \nrelationships, maintain discipline in our volume and margin choices, \nimprove productivity, and deliver measurable customer, risk and \nfinancial benefits from our investments. Our capital, funding and \nliquidity positions provide flexibility and resilience as conditions evolve.\nChief Executive Officer, Matt Comyn\nNet profit after tax\n$10,911m\n$10,982m\nStatutory NPAT2\nCash NPAT2\n8% on FY25\n7% on FY25\n2% on 1H26\n2% on 1H26\nNet profit after tax (NPAT) was supported by \nlending volume growth in our core businesses, \nwith underlying net interest margin broadly \nstable. This was partly offset by higher operating \nexpenses primarily due to inflation and \ntechnology investments, and a higher loan \nimpairment expense due to portfolio growth and \nincreased geopolitical risk and macroeconomic \nuncertainty.\nPre-provision profit \n$16,469m\n6% on FY25\n3% on 1H26\nOur pre-provision profit was up 6% reflecting \nsolid operational performance across all of our \ndomestic businesses. \nDividend\n$5.05\nPer share, fully franked\n4% on FY25\nThe final dividend was $2.70 per share, \ndelivering a total FY26 dividend per share of \n$5.05, fully franked. The full year dividend payout \nratio is 77% of cash NPAT, within our target \npayout range of 70-80%. The Dividend \nReinvestment Plan continues to be offered to \nshareholders and for this period is expected to be \nsatisfied through the on-market purchase of \nshares.\n", "ii\nCommonwealth Bank of Australia \n\u2502 ACN 123 123 124 \n\u2502 12 August 2026 \n\u2502 Media Release 215/2026\nCommonwealth Bank Place South, Level 1, 11 Harbour Street, Sydney NSW 2000\nNet interest margin\nOperating expenses\n2.05%\n$13,755m (45.5% cost-to-income)\n3bpts on FY25\n6% on FY25\n2bpts on 1H26 \nFlat on 1H26\nMargins were broadly stable excluding growth in liquid \nassets and institutional reverse sale and repurchase \nagreements, which have broadly neutral impacts on net \ninterest income. Underlying margins were supported by \nhigher earnings on replicating portfolio and capital \nhedges, and the favourable mix impact of growth in \nbusiness lending and deposits, largely offset by lower \nlending margins. \nOperating expenses increased 6% driven by inflation, \ninvestment in technology, fraud, scams and financial \ncrime, partly offset by productivity initiatives and \nfavourable foreign exchange. Investment spend of $2,428 \nmillion was up 6% on FY25 reflecting continued \ninvestment in our technology infrastructure, modernisation \nand AI capabilities. Investment spend is expected to be \nmaintained at $2.4 billion in FY27.\nCredit quality \u2013 loan impairment expense\nFunding and liquidity \n$788m (Loan loss rate3 8bpts)\n79% Deposit funding ratio (78% Jun 25)\n9% on FY25\n132% LCR4 (130% Jun 25) 115% NSFR4 (115% Jun 25)\n47% on 1H26\nLoan impairment expense increased mainly reflecting \nportfolio growth, cost-of-living pressures and increased \ngeopolitical risk and macroeconomic uncertainty. Home \nloan and personal loan arrears increased to 0.73% and \n1.72% respectively reflecting cost-of-living pressures, \nwith personal loan arrears also impacted by seasonal \nfactors and deliberate portfolio settings across credit, \npricing and acquisition mix. Provision coverage remains \nstrong at 1.53% of credit risk weighted assets. We now \ncarry a $2.7 billion buffer relative to the losses expected \nunder our central economic scenario.\nDeposit funding remained strong at 79% of total funding, \nunderpinned by a significant proportion of our funding \nrequirements being met through stable retail and business\ncustomer deposits. Long-term wholesale funding \naccounted for 68% of total wholesale funding and during \nthe year we raised $38 billion across various instruments \nand markets. A portfolio weighted average maturity of 5.2 \nyears remains conservatively positioned. Our liquidity and \nfunding positions are appropriately managed with LCR \nand NSFR well above their minimum regulatory \nrequirements.\nCommon Equity Tier 1 Capital ratio\nShareholder return\n12.0% (APRA Level 2)5 18.3% (International)\n14.0%\n$5.05\n30bpts on Jun 25 \nReturn on equity (ROE)\nDividend per share\n30bpts on Dec 25 \n50bpts on FY25\n4% on FY25\nThe Group\u2019s Common Equity Tier 1 (CET1) ratio of \n12.0% was well above APRA\u2019s minimum regulatory \nrequirement of 10.25%. Our strong capital position and \nearnings resilience enabled us to absorb losses, \ngenerate sustainable returns and support customers. \nAcross the year we deployed 72bpts of capital into credit \nrisk weighted assets with strong volume growth \nparticularly in commercial portfolios and domestic \nresidential mortgages. The $1 billion on-market share \nbuy-back, of which $300 million has been completed, \nexpires on 12 August 2026 and will not be extended.\nThe Bank\u2019s ROE increased 50bpts to 14.0% and remains \npeer leading. The final dividend was $2.70 per share, \ndelivering a total dividend for the year of $5.05 per share, \nfully franked. We seek to pay cash dividends at strong \nand sustainable levels, target a full-year payout ratio of \n70-80% of cash NPAT and maximise the use of franking.\n", "Building a brighter future for all\nCommonwealth Bank of Australia \n\u2502 ACN 123 123 124 \n\u2502 12 August 2026 \n\u2502 Media Release 215/2026\nCommonwealth Bank Place South, Level 1, 11 Harbour Street, Sydney NSW 2000\n\u2022 Provided more than 147,000 tailored payment arrangements for customers in need \nof support6.\n\u2022 Helped our customers buy more than 150,000 homes7 and provided support for \nfirst-home buyers.\n\u2022 Invested a further $140 million in our customer service network supporting \ncommunities across Australia8.\n\u2022 Paid over $22 billion in interest to Australian savers9.\nSupporting \ncustomers \n\u2022 Invested more than $1 billion to help protect customers from fraud, scams, cyber \nthreats and financial crime10.\n\u2022 Developed AI-powered cyber defence agents \u2013 improving detection speed and \nresponse efficiency.\n\u2022 Proactively alerted customers to potential threats through ~40,000 daily fraud alerts \nand sent >5.9 million notifications via intelligent first-time payment warnings11.\n\u2022 Leading AI-powered scam intelligence capability \u2013 sharing actionable intelligence at \nscale to help protect all Australians. \nProtecting \ncommunities\nInvesting in \nAustralia\n\u2022 Backed businesses with $50 billion in funding to help them invest, grow and \nemploy people12.\n\u2022 Launched national AI, cybersecurity and digital capability initiative with OpenAI for \n1 million small businesses. \n\u2022 Maintained balance sheet strength to help support customers and financial \nstability.\n\u2022 Returned $8.3 billion to shareholders, benefitting over 14 million Australians13.\n\u2022 We are one of Australia\u2019s largest corporate taxpayers, paying over $5 billion in \ngovernment payments in FY2614.\niii\n", "iv\nFootnotes\nInvestor Relations\nMelanie Kirk\n+61 2 9118 7113\nCBAInvestorRelations@cba.com.au\n \nMedia Relations\nAdam Haynes\n+61 2 9595 3219\nMedia@cba.com .au\nInvestor Centre\nFor more information: \ncommbank. com.au/investors\nThe release of this announcement was authorised by the Board.\n1. Unless otherwise stated, the financial results are presented on a continuing operations basis and all financial comparative information has \nbeen restated to conform to presentation in the current period.\n2. For an explanation of and reconciliation between statutory and cash NPAT refer to page 3 of the Profit Announcement for the year ended \n30 June 2026.\n3. Level 2 is the consolidated banking group including banking subsidiaries such as ASB Bank Limited and CBA Europe N.V..\n6. Payment arrangements in FY26 defined at account level. Excludes Bankwest.\n7. FY26.\n8. Announced June 2026.\n9. Includes interest paid on deposits in FY26.\n10. Includes expenditure on operational processes and upgrading functionalities in FY26.\n11. Since launch in September 2024 to 30 June 2026.\n12. Business Banking business lending, new funding and drawdowns in FY26. \n13. CBA paid 2H25 and 1H26 dividends to over 790,000 direct shareholders and indirectly benefitting over 14 million Australians through their \nsuperannuation.\n14. Includes payment of corporate tax, employee related taxes, Major Bank Levy and net unrecoverable GST in FY26.\nCommonwealth Bank of Australia \n\u2502 ACN 123 123 124 \n\u2502 12 August 2026 \n\u2502 Media Release 215/2026\nCommonwealth Bank Place South, Level 1, 11 Harbour Street, Sydney NSW 2000\n"]

It is information given in summary form and does not purport to be complete. Information in \nthis presentation is not intended to be relied upon as advice to investors or potential investors and does not take into account the investment objectives, financial situation or needs of any particular investor. Investors should consider these factors, and \nconsult with their own legal, tax, business and/or financial advisors in connection with any investment decision.\nThe material in this presentation does not constitute an offer to sell, or a solicitation of an offer to buy, any securities in the United States or in any other jurisdiction in which such an offer would be illegal. Any securities of the Group to be offered and sold \nhave not been, and will not be, registered under the U.S. Securities Act of 1933, as amended (U.S. Securities Act), or the securities laws of any state or other jurisdiction of the United States. Accordingly, any securities of the Group may not be offered or \nsold, directly or indirectly, in the United States unless they have been registered under the U.S. Securities Act or are offered and sold pursuant to an exemption from, or in a transaction not subject to, the registration requirements of the U.S. Securities Act \nand any other applicable U.S. state securities laws.\nThis presentation contains certain forward-looking statements with respect to the financial condition, operations and business of the Group and certain plans and objectives of the management of the Group. Forward-looking statements can generally be \nidentified by the use of forward-looking words such as \u201cmay\u201d, \u201cwill\u201d, \u201cwould\u201d, \u201ccould\u201d, \u201cexpect\u201d, \u201cintend\u201d, \u201cplan\u201d, \u201caim\u201d, \u201cestimate\u201d, \u201ctarget\u201d, \u201canticipate\u201d, \u201cbelieve\u201d, \u201ccontinue\u201d, \u201cobjectives\u201d, \u201coutlook\u201d, \u201cguidance\u201d or other similar words, and include statements \nregarding the Group\u2019s intent, belief or current expectations with respect to the Group\u2019s business and operations, market conditions, results of operations and financial condition, capital adequacy and risk management. Any forward-looking statements \nincluded in this presentation speak only as at the date of this presentation and undue reliance should not be placed upon such statements. Although the Group believes the forward-looking statements to be reasonable, they are not certain and involve \nknown and unknown risks and assumptions, many of which are beyond the control of the Group, which may cause actual results, conditions or circumstances to differ materially from those expressed or implied in such statements. To the maximum extent \npermitted by law, responsibility for the accuracy or completeness of any forward-looking statements, whether as a result of new information, future events or results or otherwise, is disclaimed. Readers are cautioned not to place undue reliance on \nforward-looking statements particularly in light of the current economic uncertainties and disruption caused by the outbreak of COVID-19. The Group is under no obligation to update any of the forward-looking statements contained within this presentation, \nsubject to disclosure requirements applicable to the Group. \nReaders should also be aware that certain financial data in this presentation may be considered \u201cnon-GAAP financial measures\u201d under Regulation G of the U.S. Securities and Exchange Act of 1934, as amended, and \u201cnon-IFRS financial measures\u201d \nunder Regulatory Guide 230 \u2018disclosing non-IFRS financial information\u2019 published by ASIC, including Net Profit After Tax (\u201cstatutory basis\u201d), Net Profit After Tax (\u201ccash basis\u201d), earnings per share (\u201ccash basis\u201d), dividend payout ratio (\u201cstatutory basis\u201d),\ndividend payout ratio (\u201ccash basis\u201d), dividend cover (\u201cstatutory basis\u201d) and dividend cover (\u201ccash basis\u201d). The disclosure of such non-GAAP/IFRS financial measures in the manner included in this presentation may not be permissible in a registration \nstatement under the U.S. Securities Act. Although the Group believes that these non-GAAP/IFRS financial measures provide a useful means through which to examine the underlying performance of the business, such non-GAAP/IFRS financial \nmeasures do not have a standardized meaning prescribed by Australian Accounting Standards or International Financial Reporting Standards (IFRS) and therefore may not be comparable to similarly titled measures presented by other entities. They \nshould be considered as supplements to the financial statement measures that have been presented in accordance with the Australian Accounting Standards or IFRS and not as a replacement or alternative for them. Readers are cautioned not to place \nundue reliance on any such measures. \nThis Presentation includes credit ratings. A credit rating is not a recommendation to buy, sell or hold any securities and may be changed at any time by the applicable credit ratings agency. Each credit rating should be evaluated independently of any \nother credit rating. Credit ratings are for distribution only to a person (a) who is not a \u201cretail client\u201d within the meaning of section 761G of the Corporations Act 2001 (Cth) and is also a sophisticated investor, professional investor or other investor in respect \nof whom disclosure is not required under Part 6D.2 or 7.9 of the Corporations Act, and (b) who is otherwise permitted to receive credit ratings in accordance with applicable law in any jurisdiction in which the person may be located. Anyone who is not \nsuch a person is not entitled to receive this presentation and anyone who receives this presentation must not distribute it to any person who is not entitled to receive it.\n2\n", "Contents\nCEO & CFO Presentations \n4\nOverview & Strategy \n41\nFinancial Overview\n54\nHome & Consumer Lending\n77\nBusiness & Corporate Lending\n93\nFunding, Liquidity & Capital\n102\nEconomic Overview\n118\nSources, Glossary & Notes \n129\n", "Results Presentation\nMatt Comyn, Chief Executive Officer\n", "Delivering now\nBuilding tomorrow\u2019s bank today\n\u2022\nSupport for our customers and communities\n\u2022\n#1 or #2 Net Promoter Scores in all core markets\n\u2022\nDisciplined operational execution\n\u2022\nAbove system volume growth in all core markets\n\u2022\nEmbedding and sustaining Remedial Action Plan\n\u2022\nCash NPAT up 19.8%\n\u2022\nStrong balance sheet and surplus capital \n\u2022\nFinal dividend $2.00 - full year dividend $3.50 \n\u2022\n$6bn off-market share buy-back\n\u2022\nContributing to Australia\u2019s recovery by supporting customers\n\u2022\nReimagining banking through new products and partnerships\n\u2022\nInvesting to drive global best digital and technology capability\n\u2022\nSimpler, better \u2013 disciplined execution, further divestments\nOverview \nDelivering now, building for the future\n5\n", "Supporting\nOur customers and communities \u2013 simply, efficiently, effectively\n>6m\nVisits to COVID-19 support page1\n1.7m\nPersonalised reminders on COVID-19 support available\n+1,000\nStaff added to financial assistance teams during pandemic\n>250k\nLoan repayment deferrals concluded \n$157bn\nof new home lending2\n$50bn\nof new business lending2\n~$500m\nin benefits using Benefits finder3\n>800k\nCustomers contacted using natural disaster weather modelling4\nBenefits finder for \nBusiness from  \nJune 2021\nNew deferral \narrangements for \nhome loan and small \nbusiness customers \nfrom June 2021\n1. Largest \nexposure is to state-owned counterparties. \n\u2022 Portfolio is weighted towards airlines who generate the majority of \ntheir revenue from their domestic and regional travel markets.\nAircraft Operating Leases \n\u2022 The Group recognises ~$0.9bn of aircraft operating leases on \nbalance sheet. Pubs and Clubs \nperformed well post the removal of previous restrictions, however current \nlockdowns in NSW and Victoria will affect trading.  Clients will be monitored \nthrough the lockdown period and post restrictions easing.\n\u2022\nAccommodation Hotels are trading back up at varied rates depending on \ngeography and target market, albeit current restrictions will impact positive \ndomestic tourism growth. CBD assets and more remote regional locations \nreliant on international tourism are recovering slowly except those that have \nobtained COVID contracts. \n\u2022\nCafes and restaurant businesses are expected to see forward bookings and \npatronage increase as social distancing provisions are progressively wound \nback post lockdown.  Cafes located in suburban areas will benefit from work \nfrom home requirements, with CBD locations negatively impacted by this \ntrend.\n\u2022\nMaterial portfolio growth is concentrated on pub groups in NSW which carry \nlarge and well diversified portfolios. Awarded November 2020.\n135\n", "Sources and notes \nCash Profit\nThe Profit Announcement discloses the net profit after tax on both a statutory and cash basis. The statutory basis is prepared in accordance with the Corporations Act 2001 (Cth) and the \nAustralian Accounting Standards, which comply with International Financial Reporting Standards (IFRS). The cash basis is used by management to present a clear view of the Bank\u2019s \noperating results. It is not a measure based on cash accounting or cash flows. The items excluded from cash profit, such as hedging and IFRS volatility and losses or gains on acquisition, \ndisposal, closure and demerger of businesses are calculated consistently with the prior year and prior half disclosures and do not discriminate between positive and negative adjustments. \nA list of items excluded from cash profit is provided on page 3 of the Group\u2019s 30 June 2021 Profit Announcement (PA), which can be accessed at our website: \nwww.commbank.com.au/results\nImages\nMastercard is a registered trademark and the circles design is a trademark of Mastercard International Incorporated.\nApple, the Apple logo, iPhone and iPad are trademarks of Apple Inc., registered in the U.S. and other countries. App Store is a service mark of Apple Inc.\n136\n", "Glossary \nFunding & Risk\nLiquidity Coverage \nRatio (LCR)\nThe LCR is the first quantitative liquidity measure that is part of the Basel III \nreforms. It was implemented by APRA in Australia on 1 Jan 2015. It requires \nAustralian ADIs to hold sufficient liquid assets to meet 30 day net cash outflows \nprojected under an APRA-prescribed stress scenario.\nHigh Quality Liquid \nAssets (HQLA)\nAs defined by APRA in Australian Prudential Standard APS210: Liquidity. \nQualifying HQLA includes cash, government and semi-government securities, \nand RBNZ eligible securities. \nCommitted Liquidity \nFacility (CLF)\nGiven the limited amount of Commonwealth government and Semi-government \ndebt in Australia, participating ADIs can access contingent liquidity via the RBA\u2019s \nCLF. The amount of the CLF for each ADI is set annually by APRA. To access \nthe CLF, ADIs need to meet certain conditions and pledge qualifying securities to \nthe RBA.\nNet Stable Funding \nRatio (NSFR)\nThe NSFR is the second quantitative liquidity measure of the Basel III reforms, in \naddition to the LCR. It was implemented by APRA in Australia on 1 Jan 2018. It \nrequires Australian ADIs to fund their assets with sufficient stable funding to \nreduce funding risk over a one year horizon. APRA prescribed factors are used \nto determine the stable funding requirement of assets and the stability of funding.\nTroublesome and \nImpaired Assets \n(TIA)\nCorporate troublesome and Group gross impaired exposures.\nCorporate \nTroublesome\nCorporate Troublesome includes exposures where customers are experiencing \nfinancial difficulties which, if they persist, could result in losses of principal or \ninterest, and exposures where repayments are 90 days or more past due and the \nvalue of security is sufficient to recover all amounts due.\nTotal Committed \nExposure (TCE)\nTotal Committed Exposure is defined as the balance outstanding and undrawn \ncomponents of committed facility limits. It is calculated before collateralisation \nand excludes settlement exposures.\nCredit Risk \nEstimates (CRE)\nRefers to the Group\u2019s regulatory estimates of long-run Probability of Default \n(PD), downturn Loss Given Default (LGD) and Exposure at Default (EAD).\nCapital & Other\nRisk Weighted Assets \n(RWA)\nThe value of the Group\u2019s On and Off Balance Sheet assets are adjusted by \nrisk weights calculated according to various APRA prudential standards. For \nmore information, refer to the APRA website.\nCET1 Expected Loss \n(EL) Adjustment\nCET1 adjustment that represents the shortfall between the calculated EL and \nEligible Provisions (EP) with respect to credit portfolios which are subject to \nthe Basel advanced capital IRB approach. The adjustment is assessed \nseparately for both defaulted and non-defaulted exposures. Where there is \nan excess of EL over EP in either assessments, the difference must be \ndeducted from CET1. For non-defaulted exposures where the EL is lower \nthan the EP, this may be included in Tier 2 capital up to a maximum of 0.6% \nof total credit RWAs.\nLeverage Ratio\nTier 1 Capital divided by Total Exposures, expressed as a percentage. Total \nexposures is the sum of On Balance Sheet items, derivatives, securities \nfinancing transactions (SFTs), and Off Balance Sheet items, net of any Tier 1 \nregulatory deductions that are already included in these items.\nInternationally \nComparable Capital\nThe Internationally Comparable CET1 ratio is an estimate of the Group\u2019s \nCET1 ratio calculated using rules comparable with our global peers. The \nanalysis aligns with the APRA study entitled \u201cInternational capital comparison \nstudy\u201d (13 July 2015).\nDerivative Valuation \nAdjustments (XVA)\nA number of different valuation adjustments are made to the value of \nderivative contracts to reflect the additional costs or benefits in holding these \ncontracts. The material valuation adjustments included within the CBA result \nare CVA and FVA. \nCredit Value Adjustment \n(CVA)\nThe market value of the counterparty credit risk on the derivative portfolio, \ncalculated as the difference between the risk-free portfolio value and the true \nportfolio value that takes into account the possibility of a counterparty\u2019s \ndefault.\nFunding Valuation \nAdjustment (FVA)\nThe expected funding cost or benefit over the life of the uncollateralised \nderivative portfolio.\n137\n", "Contact us  \nInvestor Relations\nMelanie Kirk\nInvestor Relations\n02 9118 7113\nCBAInvestorRelations@cba.com.au\nMedia Relations\nDanny John\nMedia Relations \n02 9118 6919 \nmedia@cba.com.au\nInvestor Centre\nFor more information \ncommbank.com.au/investors\n138\n"]

FINANCIAL RESULTS\n \n5 MAY 2026\nHIGHLIGHTS\n$3.4bn\nStatutory net profit\ndown 5% on 2H25\nup 3% on 1H25\n$3.5bn\nNet profit ex \nNotable Items\ndown 1% on 2H25\nup 1% on 1H25\n \n12.4%\nCET1 capital ratio \nabove target ratio \nof 11.25% in normal \noperating conditions\n77cents\nInterim ordinary dividend \nper share, fully franked\nDisciplined execution through global unrest\nAnthony Miller, Chief Executive Officer\nThis half, we\u2019ve delivered solid operating momentum while investing for the future. Our strong balance sheet and \ndisciplined focus will allow us to support customers through global uncertainty.\nWestpac is well positioned to deal with the impacts of ongoing conflict. Our role is to stay close to customers, back them \nthrough current challenges and make sure help is there when it\u2019s needed. While our customers are resilient and stress \nlevels have declined, we've taken a prudent approach and increased our provisions.\nAcross the company, we\u2019ve started to execute with real momentum. We\u2019ve got the team in place, we\u2019re clear on what \nneeds to be done and the focus now is very simply on delivery. There\u2019s a strong sense of ownership and you can see that \ncoming through in how we\u2019re performing and serving customers.\nGrowth is solid across lending and deposits, with several highlights. We grew Australian mortgages, excluding RAMS, \nin the half at 1.2x system, with the proportion of new first party lending increasing. We are supporting Australian \nbusinesses with lending up across both business and institutional over the past year. At the same time we are managing \ncosts, which are down from the prior half.\nWestpac believes in the growth potential of regional Australia. We\u2019ve opened three regional service centres with \nanother to come. We've also launched our Community Banking Service in several regional locations. Our agribusiness \nbook has grown 15% during the year and we remain the only bank with a moratorium on regional branch closures \nthrough to 2030.\nWe know we must execute well across the board and nowhere is this more true than in our UNITE program. We\u2019re now \nsolidly in implement phase. In March we completed our first large-scale migration, creating a single wealth platform for \nadvisers on BT Panorama, and work is progressing well on creating one commercial bank.\nGetting UNITE done will help unlock the potential of this organisation and ensure we do things one way. I\u2019m confident in \nthe plan and I\u2019m encouraged by the progress we\u2019re making as a team.\nOutlook\nThe war in the Middle East is presenting challenges for some customers and the economic impact of the conflict will \ncontinue through the year. The disruption to energy supply chains has driven a rise in prices and we're seeing this flow \nthrough to businesses and households, with some sectors more affected than others.\nWe're ready to work with the Government to ensure Australia is better prepared for future events, including through \nongoing investment in a reliable, sustainable energy system. As a country, we must embrace the opportunity for genuine \nreform to ensure the nation remains competitive. Our stability sets us apart, but only when combined with more efficient \nand effective regulation. Boosting productivity must be the country's priority, particularly through an uplift in skills and \ntraining alongside a committed and inclusive adoption of AI and other emerging technologies.\n", "ASX ANNOUNCEMENT I WESTPAC 1H26 RESULT\nGrowth in our core markets1\nBalance sheet momentum was solid with both lending and deposit growth \nof 7% over the year.\nAustralian household deposit growth reflects strong transaction account \ngrowth and improved brand consideration.\nBusiness & Wealth deposits increased 5% driven by growth in transactional \nand savings balances. Focus remains on growing transactional accounts \nwith the number of new accounts up 33%.\nGrowth in Australian housing loans, excluding RAMS, was 7% with the \nproportion of new loans originated through the proprietary channel rising \nduring the year.\nAustralian business lending increased 16%. Growth in the Business & \nWealth segment was diversified with solid growth in our target sectors of \nagriculture, health and professional services. There was strong loan growth \nin Institutional driven by strengthening relationships with existing clients.\nCUSTOMER DEPOSITS ($BN)\n696.8\n723.0\n745.2\nMar-25\nSep-25\nMar-26\nLOANS ($BN)\n829.4\n856.4\n890.3\nMar-25\nSep-25\nMar-26\nStrong balance sheet\nCapital\nThe CET1 capital ratio of 12.4% is above our target ratio of 11.25%. This equates to \n$2.7\u00a0billion of capital above the target after payment of the First Half 2026 dividend.\nThe CET1 capital ratio decreased 11 basis points in the half as net profit was more than \noffset by payment of the 2025 final dividend and higher Risk Weighted Assets (RWA).\n \n12.4%\nLevel 2 CET1 capital ratio \ndown 11bps on Sep-25\nup 18bps on Mar-25\n \nFunding and liquidity\nThe deposit to loan ratio was 84.2%. Notwithstanding similar lending and deposit growth, \nhigher lending balances drove a modest decline in the ratio.\nThe March 2026 quarterly average liquidity coverage ratio of 132% and the net stable \nfunding ratio of 112% were both well above regulatory minimums.\nThe Group raised $24\u00a0billion of new long term wholesale funding in the financial year \nto date2.\n\u00a0\n84.2%\nDeposit to loan ratio \ndown 72bps on Sep-25\ndown 33bps on Mar-25\n \nCredit quality\nCredit quality metrics continued to improve as reflected in a decline in stressed exposure \nto TCE to 1.16%.\nThe revised economic outlook has been reflected in our base case provision scenario and \na new portfolio overlay has been added for energy intensive sectors. Credit impairment \nprovisions increased to $5.2\u00a0billion and the ratio of collectively assessed provisions to \ncredit RWA were higher at 1.29%.\n1.16%\nStressed exposures \nas a % of TCE \ndown 12bps on Sep-25\ndown 20bps on Mar-25\nShareholder returns\nOur solid financial performance and strong financial \nposition supported the interim dividend of 77 cents \nper share. This equates to a payout ratio of 77.1% \non a statutory net profit basis and 75.6% excluding \nNotable Items.\n9.6%\nROE \ndown 31bps on 2H25\nup 16bps on 1H25\n11.0%\nROTE excluding \nNotable Items \nup 14bps on 2H25\ndown 7bps on 1H25\n", "ASX ANNOUNCEMENT I WESTPAC 1H26 RESULT\nPriorities\nFive strategic priorities help us to deliver on our ambition to be our customers' number one bank and partner \nthrough life.\n1H26 HIGHLIGHTS\nCUSTOMER\nImproving service \nfor deeper \nrelationships\n\u2022\nProvided an additional $68\u00a0billion in new home lending, helping more Australians into \ntheir homes;\n\u2022\nStrengthened our commitment to regional Australia through branch investment, regional \ngraduate roles and extending the regional branch moratorium to 2030;\n\u2022\nIntroduced digital ID verification for customers emigrating from India, NZ and China to \ndrive new account conversions; and\n\u2022\nOffered new digital solutions to institutional clients, making foreign exchange and \ninternational payments faster and more transparent.\nPEOPLE\nCreating the \nbest workplace\n \n\u2022\nThe Amplify platform is capturing more dynamic employee insights to drive further \nimprovement in employee engagement;\n\u2022\nMicrosoft Copilot licenses and training available to all eligible employees; and\n\u2022\nProvided all employees access to a personalised learning platform and more than 20,000 \ncourses through LinkedIn Learning.\nRISK\nExcellence \nin execution\n\u2022\nContinued to invest in defences against scams, fraud and financial crime, while continuing \nto raise consumer awareness; and\n\u2022\nExpanded our use of AI to support our scams and fraud teams to detect threats \nand support customers in real-time, contributed to preventing $181\u00a0million in \ncustomer losses.\nTRANSFORMATION\nInvesting for \nthe future\n\u2022\nUNITE is simplifying our operating environment with completion of the first large-scale \nmigration to Panorama and commencement of the migration of commercial business \nbanking customers to One Commercial Bank;\n\u2022\nThe BizEdge lending platform is supporting faster business lending decisions and we \ncommenced the trial of Westpac One, a cloud-based digital platform for institutional \ncustomers; and\n\u2022\nWe are moving to a new operating model that is aligned to our priorities, with twenty \nend\u2011to\u2011end delivery units that bring teams closer to customers with clear accountability \nfor multi-year outcomes.\nPERFORMANCE\nBalancing growth \nwith returns\n\u2022\nTotal shareholder return of 31% for the year to 31 March 2026, highest of major \nbank peers;\n\u2022\nA strong financial position during a time of increasing global uncertainty allows us to \nsupport customers while accelerating execution of our strategic priorities; and\n\u2022\nWe continue to target a cost to income ratio lower than the peer average and return on \ntangible equity above the peer average by the end of FY29.\nAll amounts are in Australian dollars. There is no overall increase in total \ncapital requirements for banks.\nOn implementation of these revised prudential and reporting standards, existing AT1 capital instruments would be \nincluded in the calculation of the amount of total capital, until their first scheduled call date. Existing Westpac AT1 \ncapital instruments would reach their first scheduled optional redemption dates by 2031 at the latest.\nIn addition, effective 1 January 2027 the minimum leverage ratio requirement will be 3.25% based on CET1 capital \nreplacing the current requirement of 3.50% based on Tier 1 capital. Interest income is \ncalculated on financial assets classified within Stage 1 and Stage 2 by applying the effective interest rate to the gross carrying amount \nof the assets. Interest income on financial assets in Stage 3 is recognised by applying the effective interest rate to the gross carrying \namount net of provisions for impairment. Interest income on finance leases is recognised progressively over the life of the lease, \nconsistent with the outstanding investment and unearned income balance.  \nInterest expense also includes payments made under a liquidity facility arrangement with the Reserve Bank of Australia, the Major Bank \nLevy (Bank Levy) expense and other financing charges. \nInterest income and expense on financial assets and liabilities that are classified at fair value through the Income Statement are \naccounted for on a contractual rate basis and includes amortisation of premiums/discounts. Fees, transaction costs and issue costs \nintegral to the financial assets and liabilities are capitalised and included in the interest recognised over the expected life of the \ninstrument. This includes fees for providing a loan or a lease arrangement.  \n \nThe table below sets out the accounting impacts arising from the application of Australian Accounting Standard 139 \u201cFinancial \nInstruments: Recognition and Measurement\u201d to the Group\u2019s derivative hedging activities and other non-cash items. \n30 Jun 20\n30 Jun 19\nJun 20 vs\n30 Jun 20\n31 Dec 19\nJun 20 vs\n$M\n$M\nJun 19 %\n$M\n$M\nDec 19 %\nTotal interest income - \n \n \n", " \n98 \nCommonwealth Bank of Australia \u2013 Profit Announcement \nLending is the Group\u2019s primary business activity, generating most of its net interest income and lending fees. The Group satisfies \ncustomers\u2019 needs for borrowed funds by providing a broad range of lending products in Australia, New Zealand and other jurisdictions. \nAs a result of its lending activities the Group assumes credit risk arising from the potential that borrowers will fail to meet their \nobligations in accordance with agreed lending terms.  \nThis section provides details of the Group\u2019s lending portfolio by type of product and geographical regions, analysis of the credit quality of \nthe Group\u2019s lending portfolio and the related impairment provisions.  \n30 Jun These financial assets are held within a business model whose objective is to hold financial assets in order to collect \ncontractual cash flows. The contractual cash flows on these financial assets comprise the payment of principal and interest only. These \ninstruments are accordingly measured at amortised cost.  \nLoans, bills discounted and other receivables are recognised on settlement date, when funding is advanced to the borrowers. They are \ninitially recognised at their fair value plus directly attributable transaction costs such as broker fees. Subsequent to initial recognition, \nthey are measured at amortised cost using the effective interest rate method and are presented net of provisions for impairment. For the \naccounting policy for provisions for impairment, refer to Appendix 2.2. \nFinance leases, where the Group acts as lessor, are also included in Loans, bills discounted and other receivables. Finance leases are \nthose where substantially all the risks and rewards of the lease asset have been transferred to the lessee. Lease receivables are \nrecognised at an amount equal to the net investment in the lease. Finance lease income reflects a constant periodic return on this net \ninvestment and is recognised within interest income in the Income Statement.  \nWhen applying this effective interest method the Group has estimated the behavioural term of each loan portfolio by reference to \nhistorical prepayment rates and the contractual maturity. \n \n \n \n \n \n \n \n \n \n \n \n \n \n \n \n \n \n \n \n \n \n \n \n \n \n \n \n \n \n \n \n \n \n \n \n", " \n100 \nCommonwealth Bank of Australia \u2013 Profit Announcement \n \nOther\nHome\nOther\nAsset\nCommercial\nLoans 1\nPersonal 2\nFinancing\nIndustrial\nTotal\n$M\n$M\n$M\n$M\n$M\nLoans which were neither past due nor impaired\nInvestment Grade\n316,878\n4,095\n1,793\n93,837\n416,603\nPass Grade\n209,952\n12,988\n8,698\n103,537\n335,175\nWeak\n4,118\n1,370\n302\n4,534\n10,324\nTotal loans which were neither past due nor impaired\n530,948\n18,453\n10,793\n201,908\n762,102\nLoans which were past due but not impaired 3\nPast due 1 - \n \nBy providing loans to customers, the Group bears the risk that the future circumstances of customers might change, including their \nability to repay their loans in part or in full. While the Group\u2019s credit and responsible lending policies aim to minimise this risk, there will \nalways be instances where the Group will not receive the full amount owed and hence a provision for impaired loans will be necessary. \n \nA description of the key components of the Group\u2019s AASB 9 impairment methodology is provided in Note 3.2 of the 2020 Annual Report. \n \n \n", " \nCommonwealth Bank of Australia \u2013 Profit Announcement \n103 \n\u202f \u202f \nStable and well diversified funding sources are critical to the Group\u2019s ability to fund its lending and investing activities, and support \ngrowing its business.  \nOur main sources of funding include customer deposits, and term funds raised in domestic and offshore wholesale markets via issuing \ndebt securities and loan capital. The Group also relies on repurchase agreements as a source of short-term wholesale funding. Policies for each component are set out below: \nOrdinary shares are recognised at the amount paid up per ordinary share, net of directly attributable issue costs. Where the Bank or \nentities within the Group purchase shares in the Bank, the consideration paid is deducted from total shareholders\u2019 equity and the shares \nare treated as treasury shares until they are subsequently sold, reissued or cancelled. Where such shares are sold or reissued, any \nconsideration received is included in shareholders\u2019 equity. \nRetained profits includes the accumulated profits for the Group including certain amounts recognised directly in retained profits less \ndividends paid.  \nGeneral reserve \nIn prior periods general reserve was derived from profits and was available for dividend payments except for undistributable profits in \nrespect of the Group\u2019s life insurance business. Following deconsolidation of CommInsure Life on 1 November 2019, the Group is no \nlonger required to quarantine undistributable profits in general reserve. As a result, general reserve was reclassified to retained profits. \nAsset revaluation reserve \nThe asset revaluation reserve is used to record revaluation adjustments on the Group\u2019s property assets. Where an asset is sold or \ndisposed of, any balance in the reserve in relation to the asset is transferred directly to retained profits. \nForeign currency translation reserve \nExchange differences arising on translation of the Group\u2019s foreign operations are accumulated in the foreign currency translation \nreserve. Specifically assets and liabilities are translated at the prevailing exchange rate at Balance Sheet date; revenue and expenses \nare translated at the transaction date; and all resulting exchange differences are recognised in the foreign currency translation reserve. \nWhen a foreign operation is disposed of, exchange differences are recycled out of the reserve and recognised in the Income Statement. \nCash flow hedge reserve \nThe cash flow hedge reserve is used to record fair value gains or losses associated with the effective portion of designated cash flow \nhedging instruments. Amounts are reclassified to the Income Statement when the hedged transaction impacts profit or loss. \nEmployee compensation reserve \nThe employee compensation reserve is used to recognise the fair value of shares and other equity instruments issued to employees \nunder the employee share plans and bonus schemes. \nInvestment securities revaluation reserve \nThe investment securities revaluation reserve includes changes in the fair value of investment securities measured at fair value through \nother comprehensive income. For debt securities, these changes are reclassified to the Income Statement when the asset is \nderecognised. For equity securities, these changes are not reclassified to the Income Statement when derecognised. \n \n \n \n", " \n110 \nCommonwealth Bank of Australia \u2013 Profit Announcement \n30 Jun 20\n30 \nAfter fully franking the final dividend to be paid for the full year, \nthe amount of credits available at the 30% tax rate as at \n30 June 2020 to frank dividends for subsequent financial years \nis $2,007 million (December 2019: $1,255 million; June \n2019: $1,190 million). This figure is based on the franking \naccounts of the Bank at 30 June 2020, adjusted for franking \ncredits that will arise from the payment of income tax payable \non profits for the year and prior years, franking debits that will \narise from the payment of dividends proposed, and franking \ncredits that may not be available to be distributed in \nsubsequent financial periods.  \nThe Bank expects that future tax payments will generate \nsufficient franking credits for the Bank to be able to continue to \nfully frank future dividend payments. These calculations have \nbeen based on the taxation law as at 30 June 2020. \nDividends \nThe Directors have determined a fully franked final dividend of \n98 cents per share amounting to $1,735 million. There is no \nforeign conduit income attributed to the final dividend. The \ndividend will be payable on 30 September 2020 to \nshareholders on the register at 5:00pm AEST on 20 August \n2020. \nThe Board determines the dividend per share based on net \nprofit after tax (\u201ccash basis\u201d) per share, having regard to a \nrange of factors including: \n\uf0a7 \nCurrent and expected rates of business growth and the \nmix of business; \n\uf0a7 \nCapital needs to support economic, regulatory and credit \nratings requirements; \n \n\uf0a7 \nInvestments and/or divestments to support business \ndevelopment; \n\uf0a7 \nCompetitors comparison and market expectations; and \n\uf0a7 \nEarnings per share growth. \n \nDividend Reinvestment Plan \nThe Group has a Dividend Reinvestment Plan (DRP) that is \navailable to shareholders in Australia and certain other \njurisdictions. Shareholders can elect to participate to acquire \nfully paid ordinary shares instead of receiving a cash dividend \npayment. Shares issued under DRP rank equally with ordinary \nshares on issue. The DRP for the 2020 interim dividend, 2019 \nfinal dividend and 2019 interim dividend were satisfied in full by \nthe on-market purchase and transfer of shares, and had \nparticipation rates of 14.7%, 15.0% and 16.7%, respectively. \n \nRecord Date \nThe register closes for determination of dividend entitlement at \n5:00pm AEST on 20 August 2020. The deadline for notifying a \nchange to participation in the DRP is 5:00pm AEST on \n21 August 2020. \n \nEx-Dividend Date \nThe ex-dividend date is 19 August 2020. \n \n \n \n \n \n", " \nCommonwealth Bank of Australia \u2013 Profit Announcement \n111 \n\u202f \u202f \n \nThe Group is exposed to financial risks, non-financial risks and strategic risks arising from its operations. The Group manages these \nrisks through its Risk Management Framework (the Framework), which evolves to accommodate changes in the business operating \nenvironment, better practice approaches, and regulatory and community expectations. The Group\u2019s key risk types are credit, market, \nliquidity, operational, insurance, strategic and compliance. The framework is discussed in Note 9.1 in the 2020 Annual Report.\nThe Group\u2019s approach to risk management is described in the Notes to the Financial Statements in the 2020 Annual Report. Further \ndisclosures in respect of capital adequacy and risk are provided in the Group\u2019s annual Pillar 3 document. \nThe Group uses a portfolio approach for the management of its credit risk, of which a key element is a well-diversified portfolio. These policies are intended to \nprotect the value of the Group\u2019s operations during periods of \nunfavourable market conditions.  \nThe Group\u2019s funding policies are designed to achieve diversified \nsources of funding by product, term, maturity date, investor type, \ninvestor location, currency and concentration, on a cost effective \nbasis. This objective applies to the Group\u2019s wholesale and retail \nfunding activities. \nThe CBA Board is ultimately responsible for the sound and \nprudent management of liquidity risk across the Group. The \nGroup\u2019s liquidity and funding policies, structured under a formal \nGroup Liquidity and Funding Risk Management Framework, are \napproved by the Board and agreed with APRA. The Group Asset \nand Liability Committee (ALCO) charter includes reviewing the \nmanagement of assets and liabilities, reviewing liquidity and \nfunding policies and strategies, and regularly monitoring \ncompliance with those policies across the Group. Group \nTreasury manages the Group\u2019s liquidity and funding positions in \naccordance with the Group\u2019s Liquidity Policy and supporting \nstandards, and has ultimate authority to execute liquidity and \nfunding decisions should the Group Contingency Funding Plan \nbe activated. Risk Management provides oversight of the \nGroup\u2019s liquidity and funding risks, compliance with Group \npolicies and manages the Group\u2019s relationship with prudential \nregulators.  \nSubsidiaries within the Group apply their own liquidity and \nfunding strategies to address their specific needs. The Group\u2019s \nNew Zealand banking subsidiary, ASB, manages its own \ndomestic liquidity and funding needs in accordance with its own \nliquidity policy and the policies of the Group. ASB\u2019s liquidity \npolicy is also overseen by the RBNZ.  \nThe Group\u2019s liquidity and funding policies provide that:  \n\uf0a7 \nAn excess of liquid assets over the minimum prescribed \nunder APRA\u2019s Liquidity Coverage Ratio (LCR) requirement \nis \nmaintained. \nAustralian \nAuthorised \nDeposit-taking \nInstitutions (ADIs) are required to meet a 100% LCR, \ncalculated as the ratio of high quality liquid assets to 30 day \nnet cash outflows projected under a prescribed stress \nscenario;  \n\uf0a7 \nA surplus of stable funding from various sources, as \nmeasured by APRA\u2019s Net Stable Funding Ratio (NSFR), is \nmaintained. The NSFR is calculated by applying factors \nprescribed by APRA to assets and liabilities to determine a \nratio of required stable funding to available stable funding \nwhich must be greater than 100%;  \n\uf0a7 \nAdditional internal funding and liquidity metrics are \ncalculated and stress tests in addition to the LCR are run;  \n\uf0a7 \nShort and long-term wholesale funding limits are \nestablished, monitored and reviewed regularly;  \n\uf0a7 \nThe Group\u2019s wholesale funding market capacity is regularly \nassessed and used as a factor in funding strategies;  \n\uf0a7 \nBalance Sheet assets that cannot be liquidated quickly are \nfunded with stable deposits or term borrowings that meet \nminimum maturity requirements with appropriate liquidity \nbuffers;  \n\uf0a7 \nLiquid assets are held in Australian dollar and foreign \ncurrency denominated securities in accordance with \nexpected requirements;  \n\uf0a7 \nThe Group has three categories of liquid assets within its \ndomestic liquid assets portfolio. The first includes cash, and \nGovernment and Australian semi-government securities. \nThe second includes Negotiable Certificates of Deposit, \nbank term securities, supranational bonds, Australian \nResidential Mortgage Backed Securities (RMBS) and other \nsecurities that meet the RBA criteria for purchases under \nrepurchase agreements. The final category is internal \nRMBS, being mortgages that have been securitised but \nretained by the Bank, that are repo-eligible with the RBA \nusing the Committed Liquidity Facility (CLF) and the Term \nFunding Facility (TFF); and  \n\uf0a7 \nOffshore branches and subsidiaries adhere to liquidity \npolicies and hold appropriate foreign currency liquid assets \nto meet required regulations.  \nThe Group\u2019s key funding tools include:  \n\uf0a7 \nConsumer retail funding base, which includes a wide range \nof retail transaction accounts, savings accounts and term \ndeposits for individual consumers;  \n\uf0a7 \nSmall business customer and institutional deposit base; \n\uf0a7 \nWholesale domestic and international funding programmes, \nwhich include Australian dollar Negotiable Certificates of \nDeposit, US and Euro Commercial Paper programmes, \nAustralian \ndollar \nDomestic \nDebt \nProgramme, \nUS \nExtendible Notes programmes, US Medium-Term Note \nprogrammes, Euro Medium-Term Note Programme, multi \njurisdiction Covered Bond Programme and Medallion \nsecuritisation programmes; and \n\uf0a7 \nAccess to the RBA Term Funding Facility (TFF). \nThe Group\u2019s key liquidity tools include:  \n\uf0a7 \nA regulatory liquidity management reporting system \ndelivering granular customer and product type information \nto inform business decision making, and product \ndevelopment, resulting in a greater awareness of the \nliquidity risk-adjusted value of banking products;  \n\uf0a7 \nA liquidity management model that allows forecasting of \nliquidity needs on a daily basis;  \n\uf0a7 \nAn additional liquidity management model that implements \nthe established prudential liquidity requirements. This \nmodel is calibrated with a series of \u2018stress\u2019 liquidity crisis \nscenarios, incorporating both systemic and idiosyncratic \ncrisis assumptions, such that the Group will have sufficient \nliquid assets available to ensure it meets all of its \nobligations as and when they fall due;  \n\uf0a7 \nCentral bank repurchase agreement facilities including the \nRBA\u2019s CLF that provide the Group with the ability to borrow \nfunds on a secured basis, even when normal funding \nmarkets are unavailable; and  \n\uf0a7 \nA robust Contingency Funding Plan that is regularly tested \nso that it can be quickly activated when required. \n \n", " \nCommonwealth Bank of Australia \u2013 Profit Announcement \n117 \n\u202f \u202f \nReason for establishment: The Group conducts an asset \nsecuritisation program that transfers assets to Special Purpose \nVehicles (SPV) and issues asset-backed securities to \ninvestors. The Group securitises modest amounts of \nresidential home loans to issue residential mortgage-backed \nsecurities and also issues covered bonds to diversify the \nGroup\u2019s wholesale funding. \nControl factors: The Group manages these SPVs, services \nassets in the SPVs, provides interest rate and currency \nhedging, or provides other facilities such as liquidity facilities. \nThe Group retains the risks associated with the provision of \nthese services. The Group is also entitled to any residual \nincome from the SPVs after all payments due to investors and \ncosts of the program have been met, where the Group is the \nincome unitholder. \nAsset-backed securities are debt securities where the cash \nflow is dependent on the performance of the assets assigned \nto SPVs, which may consist of residential mortgages, \ncommercial mortgages or other types of receivables. The \nGroup has acquired asset-backed securities primarily as part \nof its trading activities (classified as Trading assets), liquidity \nmanagement (classified as Amortised Cost investments), and \nbalance sheet holdings (classified as Fair Value Through Other \nComprehensive Income investments).  \nThe primary source of repayment of the debt instruments is the \ncash flow from the underlying assets. Investors in the debt \ninstruments have no recourse to the general assets of the \nsponsor (except in the case of covered bonds where investors \nhave recourse to both the underlying pool and the sponsor for \nrepayment of principal and interest). The majority of the \nGroup\u2019s asset-backed securities portfolio consists of notes \nexternally rated AAA. \nThe Group invests in or establishes SPVs in the ordinary \ncourse of business, primarily to provide funding and financial \nservices for its customers. These SPVs are consolidated in the \nFinancial Statements whenever they meet the criteria of \ncontrol as outlined in Note 4.4 to the Financial Statements of \nthe 2020 Annual Report. \nThe definition of control depends upon substance rather than \nform and accordingly, determination of the existence of control \ninvolves management judgement. The Group assesses, at \ninception and periodically, whether an SPV should be \nconsolidated based on the power the Group has over relevant \nactivities of the entity, and the significance of the Group\u2019s \nexposure to variable returns of the structured entity. \nThe lending and investment arrangements are entered into \nunder the Group\u2019s approved lending criteria and are subject to \nappropriate credit approval processes. The assets arising from \nthese financing activities are generally included in receivables \nfrom financial institutions, investment securities or Loans, bills \ndiscounted and other receivables. Exposures in the form of \nguarantees or undrawn credit lines are included within \ncontingent liabilities and credit related commitments.  \nControl factors: The Group may manage these vehicles, hold \nminor amounts of capital, provide financing or transact \nderivatives with these entities. These entities may be \nconsolidated by the Group. \nLeveraged Finance \nThe Group provides leveraged finance to companies.  This can \ninclude companies acquired or owned by private equity \nsponsors which are highly leveraged, primarily domiciled in \nAustralia and New Zealand and exhibit stable and established \nearnings providing the ability to reduce borrowing levels.  \nThe Group\u2019s exposure to firms owned by private equity \nsponsors is well diversified across industries and private equity \nsponsors. All highly leveraged debt facilities provided to private \nequity sponsors are senior with first ranking security over the \ncash flows and assets of the businesses. \nHedge Funds \nThere were no material movements in exposures to hedge \nfunds during the current year and these exposures are not \nconsidered to be material. \nCollateralised Debt Obligations (CDOs) and Credit \nLinked Notes \nThe Group has no material direct or indirect exposure to CDOs \nor credit linked notes. \n  \n \n \n \n \n \n \n \n \n \n \n \n \n \n \n \n", " \n118 \nCommonwealth Bank of Australia \u2013 Profit
