\nCompletion of sale of Life insurance business in \nNew Zealand \nOn 21 September 2017, the Group announced the sale of \n100% of its New Zealand life insurance business (Sovereign) \nto AIA Group Limited (AIA) for $1.3 billion. The sale agreement \nincludes a long-term partnership with AIA for the provision of \nlife insurance products to customers in New Zealand. The sale \nof Sovereign completed on 2 July 2018, resulting in a total \npost-tax gain of $117 million (net of transaction and separation \ncosts). This includes $135 million post-tax gain net of \ntransaction and separation costs recognised during the year \nended 30 June 2019, and $18 million post-tax transaction and \nseparation costs recognised during the year ended 30 June \n2018. \n \n \n \nCompletion of sale of TymeDigital SA \nOn 1 November 2018, the Group completed the sale of \nCommonwealth Bank of South Africa (Holding Company) \nLimited (TymeDigital SA) to the minority shareholder, African \nRainbow Capital, resulting in a total post-tax loss of \n$113 million.  \nCompletion of sale of Colonial First State Global \nAsset Management \nOn 31 October 2018, the Group announced the sale of \nColonial First State Global Asset Management (CFSGAM) to \nMitsubishi UFJ Trust and Banking Corporation (MUTB). The \nsale of CFSGAM completed on 2 August 2019, resulting in a \ntotal post-tax gain of $1,617 million (net of transaction and \nseparation costs). This includes a $1,688 million post-tax gain \nnet of transaction and separation costs recognised during the \nhalf year ended 31 December 2019, and $71 million of post-tax \ntransaction and separation costs recognised during the year \nended 30 June 2019. \nCompletion of sale of Count Financial \nOn 13 June 2019, the Group announced the sale of its 100% \ninterest in Count Financial Limited (Count Financial) to \nCountPlus Limited (CountPlus) for $2.5 million. The sale \ncompleted on 1 October 2019, resulting in a post-tax gain of \n$19 million (net of transaction and separation costs). This \nincludes a post-tax gain of $52 million (net of transaction and \nseparation costs) recognised during the half year ended \n31 December 2019, and post-tax impairment losses of \n$26 million and post-tax transaction and separation costs of \n$7 million recognised during the half year ended 30 June \n2019. Upon completion, the Group provided an indemnity to \nCountPlus capped at $200 million, which was increased to \n$300 million on 29 July 2020. Refer to Note 7.1 of the 2020 \nAnnual Report for further information. As Count Financial did \nnot constitute a major line of the Group\u2019s business, it was not \nclassified as a discontinued operation. \nCompletion of sale of PT Commonwealth Life \nOn 23 October 2018, the Group announced the sale of its 80% \ninterest in its Indonesian life insurance business, PT \nCommonwealth Life (PTCL), to FWD Group (FWD). The sale \nof PTCL completed on 4 June 2020, resulting in a total post-\ntax gain of $109 million (net of transaction costs). As part of \nthe sale, CBA\u2019s Indonesian banking subsidiary, PT Bank \nCommonwealth (PTBC), has entered into a 15 year life \ninsurance distribution partnership with FWD.  \nUpdate on Aligned Advice businesses \nOn 7 August 2019, CBA confirmed it would commence the \nassisted closure of Financial Wisdom Limited (Financial \nWisdom) and allow Commonwealth Financial Planning \nLimited-Pathways (CFP-Pathways) advisers to transition to a \nself-licensing arrangement or move to another licensee. The \nGroup ceased providing licensee services through CFP \nPathways in March 2020 and through Financial Wisdom in \nJune 2020. As Financial Wisdom and CFP-Pathways did not \nconstitute a major line of the Group\u2019s business, they were not \nclassified as discontinued operations.  \n \n \n \n", " \n124 \nCommonwealth Bank of Australia \u2013 Profit Announcement \nSale of Australian Investment Exchange Limited \n(AUSIEX) \nOn 28 April 2020, the Group announced the sale of its \nsubsidiary, Australian Investment Exchange Limited (AUSIEX), \nto Nomura Research Institute (NRI). AUSIEX trades under the \nbrand name CommSec Advisor Services. On completion, the \nGroup is expected to receive proceeds of approximately \n$85 million, subject to completion adjustments. The sale is \nsubject to Australian regulatory approvals and other conditions, \nand is expected to complete in the first half of calendar year \n2021. As AUSIEX did not constitute a major line of the Group\u2019s \nbusiness, it was not classified as a discontinued operation.  \nSale of interest in Colonial First State \nOn 13 May 2020, the Group entered into an agreement to sell \na 55% interest in Colonial First State (CFS) to KKR. On \ncompletion, the Group is expected to receive proceeds of \napproximately $1.7 billion, subject to completion adjustments. \nThe sale is subject to Australian regulatory approvals, and is \nexpected to complete in the first half of calendar year 2021. \nSale of Life insurance business in Australia and \nBoCommLife  \nOn 21 September 2017, the Group entered into an agreement \nto sell 100% of its life insurance businesses in Australia \n(CommInsure Life) and New Zealand (Sovereign) to AIA Group \nLimited (AIA). On 23 May 2018, the Group announced the sale \nof its 37.5% equity interest in BoCommLife Insurance \nCompany Limited (BoCommLife) to MS&AD Insurance Group \nHoldings (MS&AD) 1, which is subject to Chinese regulatory \napprovals. The sale is expected to be completed in the second \nhalf of calendar year 2020.  \nOn \n1 \nNovember \n2019, \nthe \nGroup \nannounced \nthe \nimplementation of a joint cooperation agreement (JCA) which \nresulted in the full economic interests associated with \nCommInsure Life being transferred to AIA and AIA obtaining \ndirect management and control of the business (excluding the \nGroup\u2019s 37.5% equity interest in BoCommLife). As a result, \nCommInsure Life (excluding BoCommLife) was deconsolidated \nand derecognised on 1 November 2019.  \nThe Group and AIA remain fully committed to completing the \ndivestment of CommInsure Life through either a share sale or \na statutory asset transfer. In the event of a share sale, the \ndivestment is expected to complete shortly following the \ncompletion of the sale of the Group\u2019s 37.5% equity interest in \nBoCommLife. In the event of a statutory asset transfer, the \ndivestment is expected to complete in the first half of calendar \nyear 2021. \nThe aggregate proceeds, which will be received in instalments \nunder the JCA, are $2,375 million, before completion account \nadjustments, \nand \nincludes \nfour \npartnership \nmilestone \npayments of $50 million each. The Group recognised a total \npost-tax loss of $316 million on the deconsolidation and \nplanned divestment of CommInsure Life. This includes a \n$116 million \npost-tax \nloss \non \ndeconsolidation, \nnet \nof \ntransaction and separation costs recognised during the half \nyear ended 31 December 2019. Post-tax transaction and \nseparation costs of $82 million and $118 million were \nrecognised during the years ended 30 June 2019 and 30 June \n2018, respectively. As at 30 June 2020, the Group has \nreceived total proceeds of $1,608 million, including partnership \nmilestone payments of $100 million.  \n \nProvisions for customer remediation require significant levels \nof estimation and judgement. The amount raised depends on a \nnumber of different assumptions, such as the number of years \nimpacted, the forecast refund rate and the average cost per \ncase. The Group is committed to comprehensively and \nefficiently addressing the full range of remediation issues \nimpacting customers of the Banking and Wealth Management \nbusinesses. Significant resources have been committed to a \ncomprehensive program of work, to ensure that all issues are \nidentified and addressed. \nAligned Advice remediation \u2013 ongoing service fees \nAligned advisors were not employed by the Group but were \nrepresentatives authorised to provide financial advice under \nthe licences of the Group\u2019s subsidiaries, Financial Wisdom \nLimited (FWL), Count Financial Limited (Count Financial) and \nCommonwealth Financial Planning Limited-Pathways (CFP-\nPathways). \nThe Group completed the sale of Count Financial to CountPlus \nLimited (CountPlus) on 1 October 2019, and ceased providing \nlicensee services through CFP-Pathways and Financial \nWisdom in March and June 2020, respectively. The Bank \nentered into reimbursement agreements with Financial \nWisdom and CFP-Pathways, and an indemnity deed with \nCountPlus, to cover potential remediation of past issues \nincluding \nongoing \nservice \nfees. \nFor \ndetails \non \nthe \nreimbursement agreements and the indemnity deed, refer to \nNote 11.2 of the 2020 Annual Report. \nDuring the year ended 30 June 2020, the Group raised a net \nincrease in the provision for Aligned Advice remediation issues \nand program costs of $300 million, including ongoing service \nfees charged where no service was provided. As at 30 June \n2020, the provision held by the Group in relation to Aligned \nAdvice remediation was $804 million (30 June 2019: \n$534 million). The provision includes $418 million for customer \nfee refunds (30 June 2019: $251 million), $280 million for \ninterest on fees subject to refunds (30 June 2019: $123 million) \nand $106 million for costs to implement the remediation \nprogram (30 June 2019: $160 million). \nThe Group\u2019s estimate of the proportion of fees to be refunded \nis based on sample testing and assumes a refund rate of 37% \n(30 June 2019: 24%). This compares to a refund rate of 22%, \nwhich \nwas \npaid \nfor \nour \nsalaried \nadvisors. \nAn \nincrease/(decrease) in the failure rate by 1% would result in an \nincrease/(decrease) \nin \nthe \nprovision \nof \napproximately \n$20 million (30 June 2019: $15 million). \nThe Group is continuing to engage with ASIC in relation to its \nremediation approach. \nBanking and other Wealth customer remediation \nDuring the year ended 30 June 2020, the Group raised an \nadditional $94 million provision for Banking and other Wealth \ncustomer remediation programs (30 June 2019: $384 million). \nAs at 30 June 2020, the provision held by the Group in relation \nto Banking and other Wealth customer remediation was \n$227 million (30 June 2019: $384 million). \n \n \n \n1 \nMS&AD Insurance Group Holdings is the ultimate parent company of \nMitsui Sumitomo Insurance Co. Ltd. \n", " \nCommonwealth Bank of Australia \u2013 Profit Announcement \n125 \n\u202f \u202f \nThe provision for banking remediation includes an estimate of \nrefunds (including interest) to customers relating to business \nbanking products (including bank guarantees, cash deposit \naccounts, merchants billing and certain commercial lending \nproducts), retail banking products (including home loans and \nother retail products), and the related program costs. \nThe Wealth remediation provision includes an estimate of \nrefunds (including interest) relating to advice quality, \ntransactions with deceased estates, the Loan Protection \nInsurance product, certain superannuation and other products, \nand the related program costs.  \nThe Group is party to a number of legal proceedings, and the \nsubject of various investigations and reviews. Provisions have \nbeen raised where indicated in accordance with the principles \noutlined in the accounting policy section of this note. \nThe main litigated claims against the Group as at 30 June \n2020 are summarised below. \nShareholder class actions \nIn October 2017 and June 2018 two separate shareholder \nclass action proceedings were filed against CBA in the Federal \nCourt of Australia, alleging breaches of CBA\u2019s continuous \ndisclosure obligations and misleading and deceptive conduct \nin relation to the subject matter of the civil penalty proceedings \nbrought against CBA by the Australian Transaction Reports \nand Analysis Centre (AUSTRAC). The AUSTRAC proceedings \nconcerned contraventions of the Anti-Money Laundering and \nCounter-Terrorism Financing Act 2006 (Cth). \nThe resolution of the AUSTRAC civil penalty proceedings was \napproved by the Federal Court of Australia on 20 June 2018 \nwith CBA paying a penalty of $700 million and legal costs. \nIt is alleged in the class actions that CBA shareholders who \nacquired an interest in CBA shares between 16 June 2014 and \n3 August 2017 suffered losses as a result of the alleged \nconduct. The two class actions are being case managed \ntogether, with a single harmonised statement of claim. CBA \ndenies the allegations made against it, and it is currently not \npossible to determine the ultimate impact of these claims, if \nany, on the Group. The Group has provided for legal costs \nexpected to be incurred in the defence of the claims. \nSuperannuation class action \nThe Group is also defending four class action claims in relation \nto superannuation products. \nOn 9 October 2018, a class action was filed against Colonial \nFirst State Investments Limited (CFSIL) and CBA in the \nFederal Court of Australia. The claim initially related to \ninvestment in cash and deposit options (which are cash and \ndeposit products provided by CBA) in the Colonial First State \nFirst Choice Superannuation Trust and Commonwealth \nEssential Super. A second further amended statement of claim \nand amended application was filed on 2 June 2020, joining \nAvanteos Investments Limited (AIL) as a party in respect of \nclaims regarding the FirstWrap Pooled Cash Account and \nexpanding the existing claims made against CFSIL and CBA. \nThe main claims are that members invested in these cash and \ndeposit options received lower interest rates than they could \nhave received had CFSIL/AIL offered similar products made \navailable in the market by another bank with comparable risk  \n \nand that CFSIL/AIL retained the margin that arises through the  \ninternal transfer pricing process in respect of deposits made \nwith CBA, for their own benefit. It is claimed CFSIL/AIL \nbreached their duties as a trustee of the funds, CFSIL \nbreached its duties as a Responsible Entity of the underlying \nmanaged investment schemes and that CBA was involved in \nCFSIL/AIL\u2019s breaches. CBA, CFSIL and AIL deny the \nallegations and are defending the proceedings. The Court has \nordered the parties to participate in a mediation of this matter, \nwhich is scheduled to take place on 3 September 2020. \nOn 18 October 2019 another class action was commenced \nagainst CFSIL in the Federal Court of Australia. The claim \nrelates to certain fees charged to members of the Colonial First \nState First Choice Superannuation Trust. It is alleged that \nCFSIL \nbreached \nits \nduties \nas \ntrustee \nand \nacted \nunconscionably because it failed, between 2013 and 2019, to \ntake steps to avoid the payment of grandfathered commissions \nto financial advisers, which would have resulted in a reduction \nof the fees paid by members in respect of whom those \ncommissions were paid. CFSIL denies the allegations and is \ndefending the proceedings. The Court has ordered the parties \nto participate in a mediation of this matter by 18 December \n2020. \nOn 24 October 2019 a third class action was filed against \nCFSIL and a former executive director of CFSIL in the Federal \nCourt of Australia, relating to alleged contraventions of \nstatutory obligations under superannuation law and trustee \nbreaches in the period 2013 to 2017. The class action relates \nto the transfer of certain default balances held by members of \nFirstChoice Employer Super to a MySuper product. The key \nallegation is that members should have been transferred to a \nMySuper product earlier than they were, and that the alleged \nfailure to effect the transfer as soon as reasonably practical \ncaused affected members to pay higher fees and receive lower \ninvestment returns during the point of delay. The allegations \nare denied and CFSIL and its former director are defending the \nclass action. The Court has ordered the parties to participate in \na mediation which will take place on 20 November 2020. \nOn 22 January 2020, a fourth class action was filed against \nCFSIL and The Colonial Mutual Life Assurance Society Limited \n(CMLA) in the Federal Court of Australia. The class action \nalleges that CFSIL did not act in the best interests of members \nand breached its trustee duties when taking out group \ninsurance policies obtained from CMLA. The key allegation is \nthat CFSIL entered into and maintained insurance policies with \nCMLA on terms that were less favourable to members than \nwould have reasonably been available in the market. It is \nalleged that CMLA was knowingly involved in CFSIL\u2019s \ncontraventions \nas \ntrustee \nand \nprofited \nfrom \nthose \ncontraventions. The allegations are denied and CFSIL and \nCMLA are defending the class action. \nThe Group has provided for the legal costs expected to be \nincurred in the defence of the claims. \nUS BBSW class action \nIn 2016 a class action was commenced in the United States \nDistrict Court in New York against CBA, other banks and two \nbrokers, claiming a conspiracy among competitors to \nmanipulate the BBSW benchmark for mutual gain. The claims \ninclude allegations that United States racketeering and \nantitrust legislation have been contravened. In November \n2018, the Court dismissed the claims against CBA and the  \n", " \n126 \nCommonwealth Bank of Australia \u2013 Profit Announcement \nother foreign defendants, but in April 2019, an amended \ncomplaint was filed that included new allegations and added a \nnew named plaintiff. The defendants applied to the Court to \ndismiss the amended complaint. In February 2020, the judge \ndetermined that the new named plaintiff\u2019s claims could proceed \nagainst CBA and nine other banks. CBA denies the allegations \nand will be defending the class action. The breadth of the \nputative class (if any) that may be allowed to claim against \nCBA will not be determined until at the earliest August 2021. \nThe preparation of the substantive proceedings has now \ncommenced. \nIt is currently not possible to determine the ultimate impact of \nthis claim, if any, on the Group. The Group has provided for \nlegal costs expected to be incurred in the defence of this class \naction. \nConsumer credit insurance class action \nOn 10 June 2020 a class action was commenced against CBA \nand CMLA in the Federal Court of Australia. The claim relates \nto consumer credit insurance for credit cards and personal \nloans that was sold between 1 January 2010 and 7 March \n2018. The class action alleges that CBA and CMLA engaged \nin unconscionable and misleading or deceptive conduct, failed \nto act in the best interests of customers and provided them \nwith inappropriate advice. In particular, it is alleged that some \ncustomers were excluded from claiming certain benefits under \nthe policies and the insurance was therefore unsuitable or of \nno value. Allegations are also made in relation to the manner \nin which the insurance was sold. The Court has made orders \nrequiring CBA and CMLA to file their responses to the claim by \n21 September 2020. It is currently not possible to determine \nthe ultimate impact of this claim, if any, on the Group. The \nGroup has provided for legal costs expected to be incurred in \nthe defence of this class action. \nCFSIL My Super \nOn 17 March 2020 ASIC commenced civil penalty proceedings \nagainst CFSIL in the Federal Court of Australia for alleged \nbreaches of the Australian Securities and Investments \nCommission Act 2001 (Cth) and Corporations Act 2001 (Cth) \n(Corporations Act) arising from communications with members \nof the FirstChoice Fund. In 2012, the Australian Government \npassed legislation requiring trustees, such as CFSIL to allocate \nmember contributions to a default \u201cMySuper\u201d superannuation \nproduct in certain circumstances. ASIC alleges, amongst other \nthings, that CFSIL communicated with members both in \ntemplate letters and on telephone calls, in a misleading or \ndeceptive manner regarding the provision of investment \ndirections to stay with CFSIL\u2019s FirstChoice Fund rather than \ntransitioning to CFSIL\u2019s MySuper product. \nCFSIL filed its response to the claim on 17 July 2020. It is \ncurrently not possible to determine the ultimate impact of this \nclaim. The Group has provided for legal costs expected to be \nincurred in the defence of this claim. \nCommonwealth Essential Super \nOn 22 June 2020 ASIC commenced civil penalty proceedings \nagainst CFSIL and CBA in the Federal Court of Australia for \nalleged contraventions of the conflicted remuneration provisions \nin the Corporations Act relating to the arrangements between  \n \n \n \nCFSIL and CBA for the distribution of Commonwealth Essential \nSuper (CES). CES is a superannuation product issued by \nCFSIL. It is currently not possible to determine the ultimate \nimpact of this claim, if any, on the Group. The Group has \nprovided for legal costs expected to be incurred in the defence of \nthis claim.  \nThe Group undertakes ongoing compliance activities, including \nbreach reporting, reviews of products, advice, conduct and \nservices provided to customers, as well as interest, fees and \npremiums charged. Some of these activities have resulted in \nremediation programs and where required the Group consults \nwith the relevant regulator on the proposed remediation action. \nProvisions have been recognised by the Group where the \ncriteria outlined in the accounting policy section of this note are \nsatisfied. Contingent liabilities exist with respect to these matters \nwhere it is not possible to determine the extent of any obligation \nto remediate or the potential liability cannot be reliably estimated. \nThere are also a number of ongoing matters where regulators \nare investigating whether CBA or a Group entity has breached \nlegal or regulatory obligations. Where a breach has occurred, \nregulators are likely to impose, or apply to a Court for, fines \nand/or other sanctions. These matters include investigations by \nAPRA and ASIC of issues which were referred to them by the \nFinancial Services Royal Commission, as well as a number of \nother matters notified to, or identified by, regulators. \nIn addition to possible regulatory action, there may also be \nfinancial exposure to claims by customers and this could include \nfurther class actions, customer remediation or claims for \ncompensation. The outcomes and total costs associated with \nsuch regulatory investigations and possible customer claims \nremain uncertain. \nThese investigations include ASIC\u2019s investigation regarding the \nAUSTRAC proceedings noted above. In September 2017, \nfollowing the commencement of the civil proceedings against \nCBA by AUSTRAC, ASIC launched an investigation in relation to \nthe Group\u2019s disclosure concerning the matters the subject of the \nAUSTRAC proceedings. ASIC is also investigating, among other \nthings, whether the directors and officers of CBA complied with \nother specific obligations under the Corporations Act. It is \ncurrently not possible to determine the ultimate impact of this \ninvestigation, if any, on the Group. The Group has provided for \nthe legal costs expected to be incurred in relation to this \ninvestigation.  \nFair Work Ombudsman (FWO) investigation \nThe FWO\u2019s investigation in relation to CBA\u2019s self-disclosure of \ndiscrepancies in employee arrangements and entitlements is \nongoing, and CBA continues to engage with FWO and respond \nto its requests for information. It is currently not possible to \ndetermine the ultimate impact of this investigation on the Group. \nCBA is continuing with its broad review of employee entitlements \nand is remediating impacted current and former employees as \nthe review progresses. We continue to update both the FWO \nand the Finance Sector Union and will provide a broader update \non progress in due course. The Group holds a provision for \nremediation and program costs related to this matter. \nNew Zealand compliance audit findings \nThe Labour Inspectorate in New Zealand is undertaking a \nprogramme of compliance audits on a number of organisations  \n", " \nCommonwealth Bank of Australia \u2013 Profit Announcement \n127 \n\u202f \u202f \nin respect of the Holidays Act 2003 (Holidays Act). On \n18 December 2018, ASB Bank Limited (ASB) received the \nLabour Inspectorate\u2019s report of its findings on ASB\u2019s compliance \nwith the Holidays Act. The findings, based on a sample of \nemployees, include that ASB has not complied with the \nrequirements of the Holidays Act by not including certain \nincentive payments in ASB\u2019s calculation of gross earnings under \nthe Holidays Act. ASB\u2019s position in relation to that finding is that \nthe application of the law is yet to be finally determined. That \nfinding, if extrapolated to ASB\u2019s entire workforce, would result in \nan estimated liability of NZD 33 million in total for the preceding \nsix years\u2019 annual holiday payments. ASB continues to engage \nwith the Labour Inspectorate on the matter. The Group holds a \nprovision for this matter. \nHome loan pricing inquiry \nIn October 2019, the ACCC commenced an industry-wide \ninquiry into home loan pricing. The inquiry involves consideration \nof a wide range of issues including the interest rates paid by new \nand existing customers, how the cost of financing for banks has \naffected bank decisions on interest rates and barriers to \ncustomers switching home loans with the focus on the period \nsince 1 January 2019. CBA is co-operating with the ACCC in its \nrequests for information. The ACCC published an interim report \non 27 April 2020. The final report from the inquiry is due by \n30 November 2020. \nOther regulatory matters \nThe following matters were significant regulatory investigations \nand reviews, which have been completed, but have resulted in \nongoing action required by the Group. \nEnforceable undertaking to ASIC (foreign exchange) \nIn December 2016 CBA provided an enforceable undertaking \n(EU) to ASIC arising from an investigation into wholesale spot \nforeign exchange (FX) trading between 2008 and 2013. The EU \nincluded the engagement of an independent expert, to review \nand assess the changes we have made to our trading operating \nmodel in recent years, including in training, procedures and \noversight. \nIt also included a voluntary contribution of $2.5 million to support \nthe further development of financial literacy education relating to \nchanges to delivery of care in the aged care sector. \nCBA provided details of the implementation of its Final FX EU \nProgram to ASIC in March 2019. The independent expert \nconducted an assessment of CBA\u2019s implementation and \nsubmitted its final expert report on 31 May 2019. The report \nhighlighted certain terms of the consolidated Final FX EU \nProgram, which were yet to be implemented, certain matters that \ncould not be assessed and some other areas for improvement. \nCBA has steps underway to address the matters raised in the \nindependent expert\u2019s report and is having ongoing discussions \nwith ASIC in respect of the FX EU Program. \nPrudential \ninquiry \ninto \nCBA \nand \nenforceable \nundertaking to APRA \nOn 28 August 2017 APRA announced it would establish an \nindependent prudential inquiry (the Inquiry) into the Group \nfocusing on the governance, culture and accountability \nframeworks and practices within the Group. The final report of \nthe Inquiry was released on 1 May 2018 (the Final Report). The \nFinal Report made a number of findings regarding the complex \ninterplay of organisational and cultural factors within the Group  \n \nand the need for enhanced management of non-financial risks. \nIn response to the Final Report, the Group acknowledged that it \nwill implement all of the recommendations and agreed to adjust \nits minimum operational risk capital requirements by an \nadditional $1 billion (an impact to risk weighted assets of \n$12.5 billion) until such time as the recommendations are \nimplemented to APRA\u2019s satisfaction. \nCBA has entered into an EU under which CBA\u2019s remedial action \n(Remedial Action Plan) in response to the Final Report would be \nagreed and monitored regularly by APRA. The Remedial Action \nPlan provides a detailed program of change outlining how CBA \nwill improve the way it runs its business, manages risk, and \nworks with regulators. The Remedial Action Plan also provides a \ncomprehensive \nassurance \nframework, \nwith \nPromontory \nAustralasia (Sydney) Pty Ltd (Promontory) having been \nappointed as the independent reviewer, and which is required to \nreport to APRA on the Group\u2019s progress against committed \nmilestones every 3 months. \nPromontory is continuing to provide APRA with quarterly \nprogress reports, and CBA is committed to report publicly on its \nprogress against the Remedial Action Plan twice a year. Six \nPromontory reports have been released by CBA. Promontory \nhas noted that the Remedial Action Plan program of work \nremains on track and CBA\u2019s commitment to implementing the \nInquiry\u2019s recommendations in a timely and comprehensive way \ncontinued to be strong with all 176 milestones on schedule to be \ndelivered by the applicable due dates. \nThe Group has provided for costs associated with the \nimplementation of the Remedial Action Plan. \nFinancial crime compliance \nAs noted above, in 2018 the Group resolved the AUSTRAC \nproceedings \nrelating \nto \ncontraventions \nof \nanti-money \nlaundering/counter-terrorism financing (AML/CTF) laws. \nRecognising the crucial role that the Group plays in fighting \nfinancial crime, it continues to strengthen and invest significantly \nin its financial crime capabilities, including in its AML/CTF \nCompliance team and through the Program of Action with \ncoverage across all aspects of financial crime (including anti-\nmoney laundering/counter-terrorism financing, sanctions and \nanti-bribery and corruption) and all business units. The Group \nhas provided for costs of running the Program of Action. \nThe Group provides updates to AUSTRAC and the Group\u2019s \nother regulators on the Program of Action implemented by the \nGroup following the civil penalty proceedings commenced \nagainst it by AUSTRAC. \nHowever, there is no assurance that AUSTRAC or the Group\u2019s \nother regulators will agree that the Group\u2019s Program of Action \nwill be adequate or that the Program of Action will effectively \nenhance the Group\u2019s financial crime compliance programs \nacross its business units and the jurisdictions in which it \noperates. While the Group is not currently aware of any other \nenforcement action by other domestic or foreign regulators in \nrespect of its financial crime compliance, there can be no \nassurance that the Group will not be subject to such \nenforcement actions in the future.  \nEnforceable undertaking to ASIC (BBSW) \nOn 21 June 2018, the Federal Court approved an agreement \nbetween CBA and ASIC to resolve proceedings concerning  \n \n", " \n128 \nCommonwealth Bank of Australia \u2013 Profit Announcement \nalleged market manipulation and unconscionable conduct in \nrespect of the bank bill market. CBA paid a civil penalty of \n$5 million and a community benefit payment of $15 million to \nFinancial Literacy Australia. It also agreed to pay ASIC\u2019s costs of \nthe investigation and legal costs. The Group provided for these \ncosts in an earlier period. \nAs part of the settlement CBA also entered into an EU with ASIC \nunder which CBA undertook to engage an independent expert to \nassess changes it has made (and will make) to its policies, \nprocedures, controls systems, training, guidance and framework \nfor the monitoring and supervision of employees and trading in \nPrime Bank Bills and CBA\u2019s BBSW-referenced product \nbusinesses. On 5 October 2018, CBA appointed EY as the \nindependent expert. CBA provided its BBSW Program of \nremediation work to ASIC and EY on 21 December 2018. EY \nreviewed \nthe \nBBSW \nProgram \nand \nprovided \ncertain \nrecommendations in its report dated 23 April 2019. CBA \nconsidered those recommendations with ASIC and EY and \ndelivered its Final BBSW Program to ASIC and EY on 23 July \n2019. \nEY delivered its report on CBA\u2019s Final BBSW Program on \n30 August 2019. Once the terms of the Final BBSW Program \nare agreed to by ASIC, that program will be implemented. The \nGroup has provided for costs associated with implementation of \nthe BBSW program. \nEnforceable undertaking to the Office of Australian \nInformation Commissioner (OAIC) \nIn June 2019, the Australian Information Commissioner \n(Commissioner) accepted an EU offered by CBA, which \nrequires further enhancements to the management and \nretention of customer personal information within CBA and \ncertain subsidiaries. \nThe EU follows CBA\u2019s work to address two incidents: one \nrelating to the disposal by a third party of magnetic data tapes \ncontaining historical customer statements and the other \nrelating to potential unauthorised internal user access to \ncertain systems and applications containing customer personal \ninformation. CBA reported the incidents to the Commissioner \nin 2016 and 2018 respectively and has since been working to \naddress these incidents. CBA found no evidence that its \ncustomers\u2019 personal information was compromised by the \nincident reported in 2016, and has found no evidence to date \nthat there have been any instances of unauthorised access by \nCBA employees or third parties as a result of the incident \nreported in 2018. \nThe Group has provided for certain costs associated with \nimplementation and compliance with the EU provided to the \nCommissioner. \nOther matters \nExposures to divested businesses \nThe Group has potential exposures to divested businesses, \nincluding through the provision of services, warranties and \nindemnities. These exposures may have an adverse impact on \nthe Group\u2019s financial performance and position. The Group has \nrecognised provisions where payments in relation to the \nexposures are probable. \n \n \n \nNot applicable. \nThis preliminary final report for the year ended 30 June 2020 is \nprepared in accordance with the ASX listing rules. It should be \nread in conjunction with any announcements to the market made \nby the Group during the year. \nThe preliminary final report has been prepared in accordance \nwith Accounting Standards in Australia. \nPricewaterhouseCoopers has audited the financial statements \ncontained within the Commonwealth Bank of Australia Annual \nReport and has issued an unmodified audit report. The Annual \nReport has been published together with the preliminary \nreport. This preliminary final report has not been subject to \naudit by PricewaterhouseCoopers. Ended\nHalf Year Ended\n \n \n \n", " \n138 \nCommonwealth Bank of Australia \u2013 Profit Announcement \nAssets under management \nAssets under management (AUM) represents the market value of assets for which the Group acts as \nappointed manager. Growth and volatility in this balance is a key performance indicator for the Wealth \nManagement and New Zealand businesses. \nBankwest \nBankwest is active in all domestic market segments, with lending diversified between the business, \nrural, housing and personal markets, including a full range of deposit products. From 1 July 2018, the\nretail banking activities conducted under the Bankwest brand have been consolidated into Retail \nBanking Services, and the business banking activities conducted under the Bankwest brand have \nbeen consolidated into Business and Private Banking. \nBusiness and Private Banking \nBusiness and Private Banking serves the banking needs of business, corporate and agribusiness \ncustomers across the full range of financial services solutions, as well as providing banking and \nadvisory services for high net worth individuals through Commonwealth Private, and equities trading \nand margin lending services through the CommSec business. Business and Private Banking also \nincludes the financial results of business banking activities conducted under the Bankwest brand. \nCorporate Centre (including \neliminations) \nCorporate Centre includes the results of unallocated Group support functions such as Treasury, \nInvestor Relations, Group Strategy, Legal and Corporate Affairs. It also includes Group-wide\nelimination entries arising on consolidation, centrally raised provisions and other unallocated revenue \nand expenses. \nCorporations Act 2001 \nCorporations Act 2001 (Cth). \nDividend payout ratio (\u201ccash \nbasis\u201d) \nDividends paid on ordinary shares divided by net profit after tax (\u201ccash basis\u201d). \nDividend payout ratio \n(\u201cstatutory basis\u201d) \nDividends paid on ordinary shares divided by net profit after tax (\u201cstatutory basis\u201d). \nDRP \nDividend reinvestment plan. \nDRP participation \nThe percentage of total issued capital participating in the dividend reinvestment plan. \nEarnings per share (basic) \nBasic earnings per share is the net profit attributable to ordinary equity holders of the Bank, divided by \nthe weighted average number of ordinary shares on issue during the period, per the requirements of \nrelevant accounting standards. \nEarnings per share (diluted) \nDiluted earnings per share adjusts the net profit attributable to ordinary equity holders of the Bank and \nthe weighted average number of ordinary shares on issue used in the calculation of basic earnings per \nshare, for the effects of dilutive potential ordinary shares, per the requirements of relevant accounting \nstandards. \nFull-time equivalent staff \nIncludes all permanent full-time staff, part-time staff equivalents and external contractors employed \nthrough third-party agencies. \nFunds under administration \nFunds under administration (FUA) represents the market value of funds administered by the Group \nand excludes AUM. Growth and volatility in this balance is a key performance indicator for the Wealth \nManagement and New Zealand businesses. \nInternational Financial \nServices \nInternational Financial Services (IFS) incorporates the Indonesian retail and business banking \noperations, and associate investments in China (Bank of Hangzhou and Qilu Bank) and Vietnam \n(Vietnam International Bank). It does not include the Business and Private Banking and Institutional \nBanking and Markets businesses in Asia. \nInstitutional Banking and \nMarkets \nInstitutional Banking and Markets serves the commercial and wholesale banking needs of large \ncorporate, institutional and government clients across a full range of financial services solutions \nincluding access to debt capital markets, transaction banking, working capital and risk management \nthrough dedicated product and industry specialists. \nInterest rate risk in the banking \nbook (IRRBB) \nInterest rate risk in the banking book (IRRBB) is the risk that the Bank\u2019s profit derived from Net Interest \nIncome (interest earned less interest paid), in current and future periods, is adversely impacted by\nchanges in interest rates. This is measured from two perspectives: quantifying the change in the net \npresent value of the Balance Sheet\u2019s future earnings potential, and the anticipated change to the Net \ninterest income earned over 12 months. This calculation is driven by APRA regulations with further \ndetail outlined in the Bank\u2019s Basel III Pillar 3 report. \n", " \nCommonwealth Bank of Australia \u2013 Profit Announcement \n139 \n\u202f \u202f \nNet profit after tax (\u201ccash \nbasis\u201d) \nRepresents net profit after tax and non-controlling interests before non-cash items including, hedging \nand IFRS volatility, Bankwest non-cash items, treasury shares valuation adjustment, and losses or \ngains on acquisitions, disposal, closure and demerger of businesses. This is management\u2019s preferred\nmeasure of the Group\u2019s financial performance. \nNet profit after tax (\u201cstatutory \nbasis\u201d) \nRepresents net profit after tax and non-controlling interests, calculated in accordance with Australian \nAccounting Standards. This is equivalent to the statutory item \u201cNet profit attributable to Equity holders \nof the Bank\u201d. \nNet Stable Funding Ratio \n(NSFR) \nThe NSFR more closely aligns the behaviour term of assets and liabilities. It is the ratio of the amount \nof available stable funding (ASF) to the amount of required stable funding (RSF). ASF is the portion of \nan Authorised Deposit-taking Institution\u2019s (ADI) capital and liabilities expected to be a reliable source \nof funds over a one year time horizon. RSF is a function of the liquidity characteristics and residual \nmaturities of an ADI\u2019s assets and off Balance Sheet activities. \nNet tangible assets per share \nNet assets excluding intangible assets, non-controlling interests, and other equity instruments divided \nby ordinary shares on issue at the end of the period (excluding Treasury Shares deduction). \nNewCo \nNewCo represents the wealth management and Mortgage Broking businesses CBA intends to exit. \nNewCo includes Colonial First State, Financial Wisdom, Aussie Home Loans and CBA\u2019s minority \nshareholdings in ASX-listed companies CountPlus and Mortgage Choice. \nNew Zealand \nNew Zealand includes the banking and funds management businesses operating in New Zealand \nprimarily under the ASB brand. ASB provides a range of banking, wealth and insurance products and \nservices to its personal, business, rural and corporate customers in New Zealand. \nProfit after capital charge \n(PACC) \nThe Group uses PACC, a risk-adjusted measure, as a key measure of financial performance. It takes \ninto account the profit achieved, the risk to capital that was taken to achieve it, and other adjustments. \nOperating expenses to total \noperating income \nRepresents operating expenses as a percentage of total operating income. The ratio is a key efficiency \nmeasure. \nOther Overseas \nRepresents amounts booked in branches and controlled entities outside Australia and New Zealand. \nRetail Banking Services \nRetail Banking Services provides banking and general insurance products and services to personal \ncustomers. Retail Banking Services also includes the financial results of retail banking activities \nconducted under the Bankwest brand. From March 2020 the Aligned Advice related businesses were \ntransferred out of the Wealth Management division and consolidated into the Retail Banking Services \ndivision. \nReturn on equity (\u201ccash basis\u201d) \nBased on net profit after tax (\u201ccash basis\u201d) and non-controlling interests less other equity instruments\u2019 \ndistributions applied to average shareholders\u2019 equity, excluding non-controlling interests, other equity \ninstruments and the treasury shares deduction relating to life insurance statutory funds. \nReturn on equity (\u201cstatutory \nbasis\u201d) \nBased on net profit after tax (\u201cstatutory basis\u201d) less other equity instruments\u2019 distributions applied to \naverage shareholders\u2019 equity, excluding non-controlling interests and other equity instruments. \nTotal Committed Exposure \n(TCE) \nTotal Committed Exposure is defined as the balance outstanding and undrawn components of \ncommitted facility limits. It is calculated before collateralisation and excludes settlement exposures on \nderivatives. \nWealth Management \nWealth Management provides superannuation, investment and retirement products which help to \nimprove the financial wellbeing of our customers.   \nWeighted average number of \nshares (\u201ccash basis\u201d) \nThe calculation incorporates the bonus element of any rights issue, discount element of any DRP and \nexcludes \u201cTreasury Shares\u201d related to investment in the Bank\u2019s shares held by the employee share \nscheme trust. \nWeighted average number of \nshares (\u201cstatutory basis\u201d) \nThe calculation incorporates the bonus element of any rights issue, discount element of any DRP and \nexcludes \u201cTreasury Shares\u201d related to investments in the Bank\u2019s shares held both by the life insurance \nstatutory funds and by the employee share scheme trust. \n", " \n140 \nCommonwealth Bank of Australia \u2013 Profit Announcement \nRetail Banking Services \nHome loans (APRA) \nCBA Loans to individuals that are Securitised Owner Occupied and Investment Home Loans.  \nAPRA Monthly ADI Statistics back series. \nHome Loans (RBA) \nCBA Loans to individuals are Owner Occupied and Investment Home Loans (including securitisation) \nas per APRA monthly ADI Statistics + separately reported subsidiaries: Wallaby Trust, Residential \nMortgage Group (APRA Monthly ADI Statistics back series). \nConsumer finance (other \nhousehold lending) \nCBA Lending to Individuals which includes: Personal Loans, Margin Lending, Personal Leasing, \nRevolving Deposits). \nDeposits from Households (APRA Monthly ADI Statistics back series). \nBusiness Banking \nBusiness lending (APRA) \nCBA Total Loans to residents as reported under APRA definitions for the Non-Financial Corporations \nsector (as per lending balances submitted to APRA in ARF720.1A ABS/RBA Loans and Finance \nLeases) (this includes some Housing Loans to Business). \nLoans to Non-Financial Corporations (APRA Monthly ADI Statistics back series). \nBusiness lending (RBA) \nCBA Business Lending and Credit: specific \u201cbusiness lending\u201d categories in lodged APRA returns \u2013\nARF720.1A ABS/RBA Loans and Finance Leases, ARF720.7 ABS/RBA Bill Acceptances and \nEndorsements, excluding sub-categories of Banks, ADIs and RFCs and governments. \nRBA Total Business Lending (adjusted for series breaks). \nBusiness deposits (APRA) \nTotal CBA transaction and non-transaction account deposit balances from residents as reported under \nAPRA definitions for the non-financial Refer to Appendix 6.2 ASX Appendix 4E on page 107 for disclosures \nunder ASX Listing Rules.  \n \nThis report should be read in conjunction with the 30 June 2024 Annual Financial Report of the Commonwealth Bank of Australia and any \npublic announcements made in the period by the Group in accordance with the continuous disclosure requirements of the Corporations \nAct 2001 and the ASX Listing Rules.  \n \nExcept where otherwise stated, all figures relate to the full year ended 30 June 2024. The term \u201cprior year\u201d refers to the full year ended \n30 June 2023, while the term \u201cprior half\u201d refers to the half year ended 31 December 2023. \n", "1. On or around.\n", "This page has been intentionally left blank \n", "", " \n \nThis page has been intentionally left blank \n", "ASX  \nAnnouncement\n", "Net profit after tax\n$9,481m\n$9,836m\nStatutory NPAT2\nCash NPAT2\n6% on FY23\n2% on FY23\n4% on 1H24\n4% on 1H24\nNet profit after tax (NPAT) was supported by \nvolume growth in our core businesses offset by \nlower lending and deposit margins. The reduction \nin NPAT was driven by inflationary increases in \noperating expenses, partly offset by a lower loan \nimpairment expense.\nPre-provision profit \n$14,956m\n2% on FY23\n4% on 1H24\nOur pre-provision profit was down 2% reflecting \ncontinued competitive pressure on margins and \ninflationary cost increases. \nDividend\n$4.65\nPer share, fully franked\n3% on FY23\nThe final dividend was $2.50 per share, \ndelivering a total FY24 dividend per share of \n$4.65, fully franked. The full year dividend payout \nratio is 79% of cash NPAT, at the upper end of \nour target payout range. The Dividend \nReinvestment Plan (DRP) continues to be offered \nto shareholders and is expected to be satisfied \nthrough the on-market purchase of shares.\n\u2502\n\u2502\ni\nFor footnotes see page iv of this ASX Announcement\n\u201cOur results demonstrate our continued focus on supporting our \ncustomers, our disciplined operational and strategic execution, \nand the strength of our balance sheet. \nMany Australians continue to be challenged by cost of living \npressures and a fall in real household disposable income. With \nslower economic growth and moderating demand, our strong \nbalance sheet allows us to continue to support our customers and \nthe broader economy, and deliver sustainable returns. We have \nmade it easier for our customers to access hardship assistance; \nprovided eligible homeowner customers with the option to \nsuspend mortgage repayments; and supported all customers with \naccess to money management tools.\nWe have remained focused on deepening our customer \nrelationships, which drives higher engagement, and a better \nunderstanding of our customers' needs to deliver superior \nexperiences. Our ongoing focus on customers has led to more \nthan one in three Australian consumers and more than one in four \nAustralian businesses naming us their main financial institution.\nWe have retained strong loan loss provision coverage, with \nsurplus capital and conservative funding metrics. Our disciplined \napproach to managing our balance sheet settings positions us \nwith flexibility and capacity for a range of economic scenarios, \nwhile continuing to deliver sustainable returns. We have declared \na final dividend of $2.50 per share, fully franked, resulting in a full \nyear dividend of $4.65.\u201d\n\u201cThe Australian economy remains resilient with low \nunemployment, continued private and public investment, and \nexports supporting national income. Higher interest rates are \nslowing the economy and gradually moderating inflation. Australia \nremains well positioned but downside risks continue around \nproductivity, housing affordability, as well as ongoing global \nuncertainty.\nWe will play our part in stimulating economic growth by lending to \nproductive parts of the economy. We will also continue to invest in \nour franchise to bring our purpose to life, building a brighter future \nfor all.\u201d\n", "Net interest margin (NIM)\nOperating expenses\n1.99%\n$12,218m (45.0% cost-to-income)\n8bpts on FY23 \n3% on FY23\n1bpt on 1H24 \n3% on 1H24\nMargins decreased year-on-year largely due to the \nimpact of competition and deposit switching, partly offset \nby higher earnings on replicating portfolio and equity \nhedges. Margins stabilised during the second half of the \nyear.\nOperating expenses increased 3% due to higher inflation \nimpacting staff costs, additional technology spend to \nsupport the delivery of our strategic priorities, and lower \none-off items. Investment spend of $2,010 million was up \n1% on FY23, as we continued to invest to modernise our \ntechnology and improve resiliency, enhance our services, \nand meet evolving regulatory requirements. \nCredit quality \u2013 loan impairment expense\nFunding and liquidity \n$802m (Loan loss rate 9bpts)\n77% Deposit funding ratio\n28% on FY23\n136% LCR (131% FY23)\n116% NSFR (124% FY23)\n7% on 1H24\nLoan impairment expense decreased reflecting our \nrobust credit origination and underwriting practices, rising \nhouse prices, and lower expected losses within \nconsumer finance. Consumer arrears increased \nreflecting the impact of higher interest rates and cost of \nliving pressures on some borrowers. Our home lending \nportfolio remains well-secured and the majority of home \nlending customers remain in advance of scheduled \nrepayments. Provision coverage remains strong at \n1.66% of credit risk weighted assets and we maintain a \n~$2 billion buffer relative to the losses expected under \nour central economic scenario.\nDeposit funding strengthened to 77% of total funding, \nwith an increase in the proportion of our funding \nrequirements met through stable retail, business and \ninstitutional deposits. Long-term wholesale funding \naccounted for 61% of total wholesale funding and \nportfolio weighted average maturity of 5.2 years remains \nconservatively positioned. Our liquidity and funding ratios \nremain well above minimum regulatory requirements.\nCommon Equity Tier 1 (CET1) capital ratio\nShareholder return\n12.3% (APRA Level 2)3 19.1% (International)\n13.6%\n$4.65\n10bpts on FY23 \nReturn on equity (ROE)\nDividend per share\nStable on 1H24 \n30bpts on FY23\n3% on FY23\nThe Bank maintained a strong capital position with a \nCET1 capital ratio of 12.3%, well above APRA\u2019s \nminimum regulatory requirement of 10.25%. As at \n30 June 2024, the Bank has completed $282 million of \nthe announced $1 billion on-market share buy-back. \nThe buy-back period has been extended by an additional \n12 months to allow for flexibility in execution, with \ncompletion expected to reduce the Bank\u2019s CET1 capital \nratio by ~15bpts4. We expect to operate with a post-\ndividend CET1 capital ratio of greater than 11.0%, except \nin circumstances of unexpected capital volatility.\nThe Bank\u2019s ROE decreased to 13.6% due to lower \nprofits. The final dividend was $2.50 per share, delivering \na total dividend for the year of $4.65 per share, fully \nfranked. The lower share count from the ~$9.3 billion5 of \nbuy-backs completed since FY22 have contributed an \nadditional ~26 cents6 to our FY24 dividend per share (at \ncurrent payout ratio).\nii\n\u2502\n\u2502\n", "\u2022 Supporting Australians\u2019 home ownership goals by helping more than 120,000 customers buy a home;\n\u2022 Lending $39 billion to support Australian businesses and help them grow; and\n\u2022 Maintaining the largest branch network in Australia, with a commitment to keep all CBA-branded regional \nbranches open until at least the end of 2026.\n\u2022 We employ over 53,000 people, of which the majority work in either Australia or New Zealand; this \nequated to over $7 billion in staff related expenses in FY24;  \n\u2022 We have invested over $800 million8 to protect our customers against fraud, scams, financial and cyber \ncrime;\n\u2022 Our NameCheck technology has been used 57 million9 times, and has prevented more than $410 million10 \nmistaken payments;\n\u2022 We have supported 201 community organisations right across Australia through our CommBank Staff \nFoundational Community Grants program; and\n\u2022 We have supported 8,983 participants through the Financial Independence Hub since inception in 2020.\n\u2022 $3,61811 in fully franked dividends related to FY24 for the average retail shareholder; \nAnalysis\t\n", " \nThis page has been intentionally left blank \n", "Commonwealth Bank of Australia \u2013 Profit Announcement \u2013 For the full year ended 30 June 2024                    9 \n", "10                    Commonwealth Bank of Australia \u2013 Profit Announcement \u2013 For the full year ended 30 June 2024 \nThe Bank\u2019s statutory net profit after tax (NPAT) from continuing operations for the full year ended 30 June 2024 decreased $615 \nmillion or 6% on the prior year to $9,481 million. The Bank\u2019s statutory NPAT (including discontinued operations) decreased $604 \nmillion or 6% on the prior year to $9,394 million.  \nCash net profit after tax (\u201ccash NPAT\u201d or \u201ccash profit\u201d) from continuing operations decreased $236 million or 2% on the prior \nyear to $9,836 million. The result was driven by flat operating income, a 4% increase in operating expenses 2 and a $306 million \ndecrease in loan impairment expense. \nOperating income  was flat on the prior year. Key movements included: \n\u2022 Net interest income decreased 1%, primarily driven by an 8 basis point decrease in Net Interest Margin (NIM), partly offset by a 3% or \n$33 billion increase in Average Interest Earning Assets (AIEA). NIM decreased by 8 basis points, primarily driven by the impact on \nlending margins from increased competition, reduced deposit earnings from competition, unfavourable portfolio mix mainly from \ncustomers switching to higher yielding deposits, and increased wholesale funding costs, partly offset by higher earnings on capital \nhedges. The increase in AIEA was mainly due to growth in home and business loans, and increased non-lending interest earning assets \nincluding higher reverse sale and repurchase agreements and liquid assets.  \n\u2022 Other operating income increased 7%, primarily driven by higher volume driven commissions and lending fee income, higher Markets \ntrading and sales income, partly offset by lower merchants revenue due to an increase in scheme costs and reduced equities income \nfrom reduced trading volumes. \nOperating expenses 2 increased 4% mainly driven by higher staff costs due to inflation and additional technology spend to support the \ndelivery of our strategic priorities, partly offset by productivity initiatives. \nLoan impairment expense (LIE) decreased $306 million, primarily driven by lower collective provisions reflecting rising house prices, \nslowing interest rate rises and an improved outlook for Consumer Finance. Home loan 90+ day arrears were 0.65%, an increase of \n13 basis points on the prior half reflecting the impact of higher interest rates on some borrowers. Credit Cards and Personal Loans arrears \nwere 0.74% and 1.50%, an increase of 14 basis points and 36 basis points respectively on the prior half, reflecting ongoing cost of living \npressures. Total provisions to CRWA is 1.66%, up 2 basis points on the prior half, reflecting an increase in collective provisioning driven \nby the impact on corporate profits from ongoing inflationary pressures and higher interest rates. \nCET1 remained stable from 31 December 2023 at 12.3%, well above the regulatory minimum of 10.25%. The movement was driven by \ncapital generated from earnings, offset by the payment of the 2024 interim dividend, higher other regulatory adjustments, higher total \nRWAs, and the impact of the on-market share buy-back.  \nEarnings per share (\u201ccash basis\u201d) decreased 1% on the prior year to 587.8 cents per share, primarily driven by the decrease in cash profit \npartly offset by the reduction of shares on issue as a result of share buy-backs.  \nReturn on equity (\u201ccash basis\u201d) decreased 30 basis points to 13.6% due to the impact of lower cash profit.  \nThe final dividend determined was $2.50 per share, bringing the total for the year to $4.65 which is equivalent to 79% of the Bank\u2019s cash \nprofit.  \nBalance sheet strength and resilience is a key priority for the Bank. The Bank has managed key balance sheet risks in a sustainable and \nconservative manner, and has made strategic decisions to ensure strength in capital, funding, and liquidity. In particular, the Bank has:   \n\u2022 Fulfilled a significant proportion of its funding requirements from customer deposits, accounting for 77% of total funding at 30 June 2024 \n(up from 75% at 30 June 2023); \n\u2022 Issued new long-term wholesale funding of $23 billion and repaid the RBA Term Funding Facility (TFF) of $50 billion. The portfolio \nWeighted Average Maturity (WAM)3 was 5.2 years (down from 5.3 years at 30 June 2023); \n\u2022 Maintained a strong funding position, with long-term wholesale funding accounting for 61% of total wholesale funding (down from 74% \nat 30 June 2023); and \n\u2022 Appropriately managed the level of liquid assets and customer deposit growth to maintain our strong funding and liquidity positions, as \nillustrated by the Liquidity Coverage Ratio (LCR) and Net Stable Funding Ratio (NSFR) being well above the regulatory minimum. \n \n \n \n \n \n \n \n \n \n1 \nThe financial results of discontinued operations are excluded from the individual account lines of the Bank\u2019s performance and are reported as a single cash net profit \nafter tax line item. Discontinued operations mainly includes transitional service agreements relating to divested entities such as CFS. \n2 \nReflecting underlying performance within operating expenses, excluding the impact from: $89 million of restructuring provision in FY24 and $212 million of \nrestructuring and one-off regulatory provision in FY23. \n3 \nThe portfolio WAM excluding the RBNZ Term Lending Facilities as at 30 June 2024 was 5.2 years. In prior periods this metric included RBA TFF drawdowns \n(excluding RBA TFF and RBNZ Term Lending Facility: 31 December 2023: 5.3 years; 30 June 2023: 5.5 years). \n", "Commonwealth Bank of Australia This was mainly \ndriven by increased restructures in the home lending and \ncorporate portfolios, which typically have lower provision \ncoverage.  \nConsumer loan impairment expense (LIE) as a percentage of \naverage gross loans and acceptances was 4 basis points, \na decrease of 3 basis points on the prior half, mainly driven by \nrising house prices and lower expected losses within consumer \nfinance, partly offset by ongoing cost of living pressures.  \n", "26                    Commonwealth Bank of Australia \u2013 Profit Announcement \u2013 For the full year ended 30 June 2024 \nHome loan 90+ days arrears were 0.65%, an increase of \n13 basis points on the prior half, as higher interest rates continue \nto impact some borrowers. and\n\u2022 EUR1,000 million in June 2024.\nTotal RWA increased $3.9 billion or 0.8% on the prior half to \n$467.6 billion, mainly driven by higher IRRBB and Credit RWA, \npartly offset by lower Traded Market Risk RWA. \nCredit Risk RWA increased $1.7 billion or 0.5% on the prior half \nto $370.4 billion, primarily driven by: \n\u2022 Volume growth (increase of $2.9 billion) across domestic\nresidential mortgages, commercial portfolios, and unsecured\nretail portfolios; and\n\u2022 Data & methodology (decrease of $0.4 billion).\n1 \nDue to rounding, numbers presented in this section may not sum precisely \nto the totals provided. \n1 \nCredit quality includes portfolio mix. \n2 \nIncludes data and methodology, credit risk estimates changes and \nregulatory treatments. \nTraded Market Risk RWA decreased by $1.1 billion or 12% on \nthe prior half year to $8.5 billion primarily driven by the removal \nof the APRA RNIV capital overlay. \nIRRBB RWA increased by $3.3 billion or 8% on the prior half to \n$43.6 billion, driven by higher basis risks. \nAs required by APS 115, Operational Risk RWA as at 30 June \n2024 and 31 December 2023 were determined based on the \nannual average value of the relevant components of the Group\u2019s \nnet income over the years ended 30 June 2023, 2022 and 2021. \nOperational Risk RWA are flat on the prior half. \n369\n370\n10\n8\n40\n44\n45\n45\n1.7\n3.3\n-\n(1.1)\nDec 23\nCredit Risk\nTraded\nMarket Risk\nIRRBB\nOperational\nRisk\nJun 24\n464\n468\nCredit\nIRRBB\nOp\nMarket\n1\n2\n", "30                    Commonwealth Bank of Australia \u2013 Profit Announcement \u2013 For the full year ended 30 June 2024 \nOn 1 January 2023, APRA implemented revisions to the capital \nframework for Authorised Deposit-taking Institutions (ADIs), to \nincrease the risk sensitivity within the capital framework, to \nenhance the ability of ADIs to respond flexibly to future stress \nevents, and to improve the comparability of the Australian \nframework with international standards.   \nThe APRA prudential standards prescribe a minimum CET1 \ncapital ratio of 10.25% for Internal Ratings-based (IRB) ADIs \nsuch as CBA, comprising of a minimum Prudential Capital \nRequirement (PCR) of 4.5% and a capital conservation buffer \n(CCB) of 5.75%, which includes a Domestic Systemically \nImportant Bank (D-SIB) buffer of 1% and a baseline \ncountercyclical capital buffer (CCyB) set at 1%1. The CCyB, \nwhich may be varied by APRA in the range of 0%-3.5%, can be \nreleased in times of systemic stress and post-stress recovery. \nThe Group expects to operate with a post-dividend CET1 capital \nratio of greater than 11%, compared to the APRA minimum of \n10.25%, except in circumstances of unexpected capital volatility. \nThe Tier 1 requirement as at 30 June 2024 was 11.75%.  \nTo satisfy APRA\u2019s loss-absorbing capacity requirements, the \nminimum Total capital ratio requirement for D-SIBs, including \nCBA, has increased from 13.75% to 16.75% effective from 1 \nJanuary 2024. From 1 January 2026, the requirement will \nincrease to 18.25%. \n1 \nIn July 2024, APRA announced that the CCyB for Australian exposures will \nremain at 1%. The Bank has limited exposures to those offshore \njurisdictions in which a CCyB in excess of 0% has been imposed. \nOn 8 July 2024, APRA released the final revised APS 117 \n\u201cCapital Adequacy: Interest Rate Risk in the Banking Book\u201d, \nwhich sets out the requirements that an ADI must meet in \nmanaging its Interest Rate Risk in the Banking Book (IRRBB), \nfollowing the November 2022 and December 2023 consultations \non proposed changes to the standard. The revised APS117 will \ncome into effect on 1 October 2025.  \nAPRA is expected to commence consultation on revisions to APS \n116 \u201cCapital Adequacy: Market Risk\u201d, and APS 180 \u201cCapital \nAdequacy: Counterparty Credit Risk\u201d in 2024 with revisions to \nboth standards expected to be implemented in 2026. \nThe Reserve Bank of New Zealand\u2019s revisions to bank capital \nadequacy requirements are being implemented in stages during \na transition period from October 2021 to July 2028. By the end of \nthe transition period, the minimum Tier 1 and Total capital \nrequirements for banks deemed systemically important, including \nASB, will increase to 16% and 18% of RWA respectively, of \nwhich 13.5% must be in the form of CET1 while Tier 2 Capital \ncan contribute up to a maximum of 2% of the Total capital \nrequirement.  \nAs at 30 June 2024, the CET1, Tier 1 and Total capital ratio \nrequirements for ASB were 9%, 10.5% and 12.5%, respectively. \nEffective 1 July 2024, the Tier 1 and Total capital ratio \nrequirements for ASB increased to 11.5% and 13.5% \nrespectively. \nOn 18 May 2023, APRA released its final Prudential Standard \nCPS 900 \u201cResolution Planning\u201d in final, which aims to ensure that \nan APRA-regulated entity can be managed by APRA in an \norderly manner where that entity is unable to, or is likely to be \nunable to, meet its obligations or suspends, or is likely to \nsuspend, payments. In such circumstances, the aim of the \nresolution is to protect beneficiaries, minimise disruption to the \nfinancial system and provide continuity of functions that are \ncritical for the economy. CPS 900 came into effect on 1 January \n2024. \nOn 1 December 2022, APRA released its final Prudential \nStandard CPS 190 \u201cRecovery and Exit Planning\u201d in final, aimed \nat reinforcing the resilience of the financial system. The new \nstandard aims to ensure that APRA regulated entities are better \nprepared to manage periods of severe financial stress. CPS 190 \ncame into effect on 1 January 2024 for banks. \nOn 24 October 2022, APRA released a letter to all APRA \nregulated entities indicating that it is reviewing the prudential \nframework for groups operating in the Australian banking sector \nto ensure it caters for the increasing array of new groups and it \nis consistently applied across different structures. APRA is yet to \nformally consult on any revisions to the relevant standards. \nOn 21 September 2023, APRA released a discussion paper \noutlining potential options for, and seeking feedback from \nstakeholders on, the effectiveness of Additional Tier 1 Capital in \nAustralia. APRA intends to follow this process with a formal \nconsultation in 2024 on any proposed amendments to prudential \nstandards.  \nOn 24 July 2024, APRA finalised its targeted revisions to ADIs\u2019 \nliquidity and capital requirements following the November 2023 \nconsultation, which aims to ensure ADIs have strong crisis \npreparedness, prudently value their liquid assets and minimise \npotential contagion risks. The changes will come into effect on 1 \nJuly 2025. \n \nDetails on the market disclosures required under Pillar 3, per \nAPRA Prudential Standard APS 330 \u201cPublic Disclosure\u201d, are \nprovided on the Bank\u2019s website at: \nwww.commbank.com.au/regulatorydisclosures\n", "Commonwealth Bank of Australia \u2013 Profit Announcement \u2013 For the full year ended 30 June 2024  \n  31 \nAs at \n30 Jun 24 \n31 Dec 23 \n30 Jun 23 \nJun 24 vs \nJun 24 vs \nSummary Group Leverage Ratio \n$M \n$M \n$M \nDec 23 % \nJun 23 % \nTier 1 Capital ($M) \n66,963 \n68,093 \n67,771 \n(2)\n(1)\nTotal Exposures ($M) \u00b9 \n1,339,175 \n1,362,098 \n1,334,426 \n(2)\n\u2013\nLeverage Ratio (APRA) (%) \n5.0 \n5.0 \n5.1 \n\u2013\n(10)bpts\n1 \nTotal exposures is the sum of on balance sheet exposures, derivatives, securities financing transactions (SFTs), and off balance sheet exposures, net of any    Tier \n1 regulatory deductions, as outlined in APS 110 \u201cCapital Adequacy\u201d. \nThe Group\u2019s leverage ratio, defined as Tier 1 Capital as a \npercentage of total exposures, was 5.0% at 30 June 2024. The result reflected a \n3% decrease in operating income and a 4% increase in operating \nexpenses, partly offset by a $270 million decrease in loan \nimpairment expense. \nNet interest income was $11,119 million, a decrease of \n$578 million or 5% on the prior year. This was driven by a \n19 basis point decrease in net interest margin, partly offset by a \n2% increase in average interest earning assets.  \nNet interest margin decreased by 19 basis points on the prior \nyear, reflecting: \n\u2022 Lower home lending margins principally reflecting increased \ncompetition; \n\u2022 Lower deposit margins mainly due to competition and \nunfavourable mix as customers shift to higher yielding savings \nand term deposits, partly offset by the benefit from the rising \ninterest rate environment; and \n\u2022 Lower consumer finance margins mainly reflecting cash rates \nincreasing more than customer rates; partly offset by \n\u2022 Higher earnings on equity; and \n\u2022 Favourable portfolio mix primarily due to the benefit of strong \ngrowth in deposits relative to assets.  \nOther operating income was $1,671 million, an increase of \n$198 million or 13% on the prior year, reflecting increased \nvolume driven foreign exchange, cards and lending fee income. \nOperating expenses were $4,802 million, an increase of \n$187 million or 4% on the prior year. This was primarily driven by \ninflation, higher staff costs including investment in call centre and \nscam \nmanagement \nresources, \nhigher \namortisation \nand \ntechnology spend, partly offset by productivity initiatives \nincluding workforce and branch optimisation. \nThe number of full-time equivalent staff (FTE) decreased by 499 \nFTE or 3% on the prior year, from 16,597 to 16,098. This was \ndriven by workforce optimisation including fewer branch, home \nloan processing and head office resources, partly offset by \nadditional resources to support increased call centre and scam \nvolumes. \nInvestment spend focused on strategic growth and productivity \ninitiatives including product and service innovation, digital \nenhancements, the Yello loyalty program and home buying \nprocess optimisation. We have also continued to invest in risk \nand compliance initiatives such as upgrading processes to \nreduce scam losses and to comply with regulations including \nOpen Banking. \nThe operating expenses to operating income ratio was 37.5%, \nan increase of 250 basis points on the prior year, reflecting lower \noperating income and higher operating expenses. \n \n \n \n1  In order to provide an underlying view of performance, the commentary has \nbeen presented excluding the impact of the General Insurance business \nfollowing the sale on 30 September 2022. \n", "Commonwealth Bank of Australia \u2013 Profit Announcement \u2013 For the full year ended 30 June 2024  \n  43 \nLoan impairment expense was $317 million, a decrease of \n$270 million or 46% on the prior year. Growth was driven by savings deposits\n(up 7%), investment deposits (up 10%) and transaction\ndeposits (up 1% including non-interest bearing balances) due\nto higher offset balances, partly offset by customer switching to\nhigher yielding deposits.\nRisk weighted assets were $176.9 billion, an increase of \n$1.3 billion on the prior year. This was primarily driven by higher \nIRRBB and Operational risk RWAs, partly offset by reductions in \nhome loan risk weights from rising house prices and increased \nlevels of prepayment. \nRetail Banking Services generated $5,197 million of organic \ncapital1 for the Group in the current year. This contributed \n114 basis points to the Group\u2019s CET1 ratio. \nCash net profit after tax was $2,668 million, a decrease of \n$19 million or 1% on the prior half. The result was driven by a 2% \ndecrease in operating income, partly offset by a $115 million \ndecrease in loan impairment expense and flat operating \nexpenses. \nNet interest income was $5,502 million, a decrease of \n$115 million or 2% on the prior half. This was driven by a 5 basis \npoint decrease in net interest margin and the impact of two fewer \ncalendar days in the current half, partly offset by a 1% increase \nin average interest earning assets. \nNet interest margin decreased by 5 basis points on the prior half, \nreflecting: \n\u2022 Lower deposit margins mainly due to competition and\nunfavourable mix as customers shift to higher yielding savings\nand term deposits, partly offset by the benefit from the rising\ninterest rate environment; and\n\u2022 Lower home lending margins principally reflecting increased\ncompetition; partly offset by\n\u2022 Higher earnings on equity; and\n\u2022 Favourable portfolio mix due to the benefit of strong growth in\ndeposits relative to assets.\nOther operating income was $823 million, a decrease of \n$25 million or 3% on the prior half, reflecting lower volume driven \nforeign exchange income and lower earnings from minority \ninvestments, partly offset by increased volume driven cards and \nlending fee income. \nOperating expenses were $2,401 million, flat to prior half. The result was driven by a 4% increase in \ntotal operating income, a 5% increase in operating expenses and \nan 11% decrease in loan impairment expense.  \nNet interest income was $7,511 million, an increase of \n$263 million or 4% on the prior year. This was driven by a 7% \nincrease in average interest earning assets, partly offset by a 10 \nbasis point decrease in net interest margin. \nNet interest margin decreased 10 basis points on the prior year, \nreflecting: \n\u2022 Lower business and home lending margins principally due to\nincreased competition; partly offset by\n\u2022 Higher deposit margins due to the rising interest rate\nenvironment, partly offset by unfavourable mix as customers\nswitch to higher yielding deposits; and\n\u2022 Higher earnings on equity.\nOther operating income was $1,062 million, an increase of \n$33 million or 3% on the prior year, reflecting:  \n\u2022 Increased volume driven business lending fee and FX\npayments income; partly offset by\n\u2022 Lower merchants revenue due to an increase in scheme costs;\nand\n\u2022 Lower equities income due to lower trading volumes and lower\naverage brokerage per trade.\nOperating expenses were $2,743 million, an increase of \n$137 million or 5% on the prior year. This was primarily driven by \nhigher technology spend, inflation, additional customer facing \nstaff and investment in product offerings. \nThe number of full-time equivalent staff (FTE) increased by 382 \nor 7% on the prior year, from 5,563 to 5,945 due to investment in \ncustomer facing and product staff. \nInvestment spend was primarily focused on further enhancing \nthe customer experience through reimagining products and \nservices, system modernisation, digitisation and automation. We \nhave also continued to invest in regulatory, risk and compliance \ninitiatives.  \nThe operating expenses to total operating income ratio was \n32.0%, an increase of 50 basis points on the prior year, mainly \ndriven by higher operating expenses, partly offset by higher \noperating income. \nLoan impairment expense was $437 million, a decrease of \n$55 million or 11% on the prior year driven by lower specific \nprovision charges, partly offset by higher collective provisions. \nProvision coverage remains above pre-COVID levels reflecting \nthe impact of higher interest rates and ongoing inflationary \npressures. \nLoan impairment expense as a percentage of average gross \nloans and acceptances decreased 4 basis points to 0.19%. \nTroublesome and impaired assets as a percentage of total \ncommitted exposure increased 39 basis points to 2.87%, \ninfluenced by weakened consumer demand and ongoing cost \npressures across a number of industries. \nKey spot balance sheet movements included: \n\u2022 Business loan growth of $14.7 billion or 11%, above system\ngrowth, reflecting growth across a number of diversified\nindustries;\n\u2022 Home loans growth was flat, below system growth; and\n\u2022 Total deposits increase (interest and non-interest bearing) of\n$1.4 billion or 1%. Balance growth was driven by an increase\nin Savings deposits (up 3%) and Investment deposits (up 2%),\npartly offset by a decrease in Transaction deposits (down 2%\nincluding non-interest bearing balances) reflecting greater\ndemand for higher yielding deposits.\nRisk weighted assets were $143.1 billion, an increase of \n$9.8 billion or 7% on the prior year. This was primarily driven by \nlending volume growth. \nBusiness Banking generated $2,572 million of organic capital 1 \nfor the Group in the current year. This contributed 80 basis points \nto the Group\u2019s CET1 ratio. \n1 \nOrganic capital generation represents cash net profit after tax less the \ncapital equivalent of the change in regulatory risk weighted assets  \n(excluding impact of FX movements on Credit RWAs as they are capital \nneutral with offsetting impact in Foreign Currency Translation Reserves) \nused to generate those profits.
