The result was driven by a \n3% increase in total operating income (2% increase excluding \nderivative valuation adjustments), a 3% increase in operating \nexpenses and a $32 million decrease in loan impairment benefit. \nNet interest income was $1,434 million, a decrease of $9 million \nor 1% on the prior year. Excluding the Markets business, net \ninterest income was $1,467 million, an increase of $56 million or \n4% on the prior year. The result excluding Markets was driven by \nan 18 basis point increase in net interest margin, partly offset by \na 7% decrease in average interest earning assets.  \nExcluding the Markets business, net interest margin increased \n18 basis points, reflecting: \n\u2022 Higher deposit earnings reflecting the rising interest rate\nenvironment;\n\u2022 Higher earnings on equity; and\n\u2022 Favourable assets mix from a decrease in lower margin pooled\nfacilities; partly offset by\n\u2022 Lower institutional lending and leasing margins due to higher\nfunding costs.\nOther operating income was $1,072 million, an increase of \n$91 million or 9% on the prior year, reflecting: \n\u2022 Higher trading income in Commodities (more than offsetting\nincreased funding costs in net interest income) and Foreign\nExchange, and increased sales volumes in Fixed Income,\npartly offset by lower trading revenue in Fixed Income and\nRates;\n\u2022 Favourable derivative valuation adjustments; and\n\u2022 Higher lending fees driven by increased volume of lending\nfacilities; partly offset by\n\u2022 Lower Structured Asset Finance revenue mainly from\nnon-recurrence of gains from asset sales in the prior year,\npartly offset by higher rental income in the aircraft lease\nportfolio.\nOperating expenses were $1,088 million, an increase of \n$32 million or 3% on the prior year. This was mainly driven by \ninflation, investment in business and operations resources and \nvolume driven operations costs, partly offset by lower technology \ncosts and productivity initiatives. \nThe number of full-time equivalent staff (FTE) increased by \n67 or 5% on the prior year, from 1,487 to 1,554 FTE, primarily \ndriven by higher business and operations resources, partly offset \nby workforce optimisation initiatives. \nInvestment spend focused on strategic initiatives and continuing \nto strengthen the operational risk, compliance and regulatory \nframework. \nThe operating expenses to total operating income ratio was \n43.4%, a decrease of 20 basis points on the prior year, driven by \nhigher operating income. \nLoan impairment benefit decreased $32 million on the prior year \nto $4 million. This was primarily driven by higher collective \nprovisions due to forward looking adjustments and the \nnon-recurrence of prior year provision releases, partly offset by \nhigher writebacks, recoveries and lower individual provisions for \nsingle name exposures.  \nLoan impairment expense as a percentage of average gross \nloans and acceptances increased 4 basis points on the prior \nyear. \nKey spot balance sheet movements included: \n\u2022 Interest earning lending assets balance decrease of\n$9.0 billion or 9%, primarily driven by a decrease in pooled\nfacilities from government sector clients utilising excess funds,\npartly offset by growth in the asset backed lending portfolio;\n\u2022 Non-lending interest earning assets increase of $10.0 billion or\n15%, driven by higher reverse sale and repurchase agreement\nbalances, and increases in the high grade bond and carbon\nportfolios in Markets;\n\u2022 Other assets and non-interest bearing liabilities decrease of\n$3.3 billion or 13% and $4.0 billion or 18% respectively, mainly\ndriven by the revaluation of derivative assets and derivative\nliabilities due to foreign currency and interest rate movements.\nDerivative assets and derivative liabilities are required to be\ngrossed up under accounting standards. This decrease was\npartly offset by timing of unsettled trades;\n\u2022 Total interest bearing deposits decrease of $10.3 billion or 6%,\nmainly driven by pooled facilities, partly offset by higher\nTransaction deposits (excluding pooled facilities) and Savings\ndeposits;\n\u2022 Due to other financial institutions increase of $3.3 billion or 22%\nmainly due to higher deposits from other banks; and\n\u2022 Other interest bearing liabilities increase of $16.6 billion or 38%\nprimarily driven by an increase in sale and repurchase\nagreements in Markets to fund higher non-lending interest\nearning assets.\nRisk weighted assets were $72.0 billion, a decrease of \n$2.8 billion or 4% on the prior year, primarily driven by reduction \nin \ntraded \nmarket \nrisk \nweighted \nassets \nfollowing \nthe \nimplementation of a new market risk engine and removal of the \nAPRA risk-not-in-VaR (RNIV) capital overlay, partly offset by \nincrease in credit risk weighted assets due to lending volume \ngrowth. \nInstitutional Banking and Markets generated $1,433 million of \norganic capital 1 for the Group in the current year. This \ncontributed 23 basis points to the Group\u2019s CET1 ratio. \n1 \nOrganic capital generation represents cash net profit after tax less the \ncapital equivalent of the change in regulatory risk weighted assets \n(excluding impact of FX movements on Credit RWAs as they are capital \nneutral with offsetting impact in Foreign Currency Translation Reserves) \nused to generate those profits. Amounts quoted exclude the payment of \ndividends. \n", "52  \n   Commonwealth Bank of Australia \u2013 Profit Announcement \u2013 For the full year ended 30 June 2024 \nCash net profit after tax for the half year ended 30 June 2024 \nwas $508 million, a decrease of $81 million or 14% on the prior \nhalf. The result was driven by a 5% decrease in total operating \nincome \n(6% \ndecrease \nexcluding \nderivative \nvaluation \nadjustments), and a $70 million increase in loan impairment \nexpense. \nNet interest income was $728 million, an increase of \n$22 million or 3% on the prior half. Excluding the Markets \nbusiness, net interest income was $740 million, an increase of \n$13 million or 2% on the prior half. The result excluding Markets \nwas driven by a 14 basis point increase in net interest margin, \npartly offset by a 5% decrease in average interest earning assets \nand the impact of two fewer calendar days in the current half. \nExcluding the Markets business, net interest margin increased \n14 basis points, reflecting: \n\u2022 Favourable assets mix from a decrease in lower margin pooled\nfacilities; and\n\u2022 Higher earnings on equity; partly offset by\n\u2022 Lower institutional lending margins due to higher funding costs.\nOther operating income was $492 million, a decrease of \n$88 million or 15% on the prior half, reflecting: \n\u2022 Lower trading income across Commodities, Carbon and Fixed\nIncome, and lower sales income in Commodities; and\n\u2022 Lower commissions due to increased merchants scheme costs.\nOperating expenses were $545 million, an increase of $2 million \non the prior half. This was mainly driven by investment in frontline \nstaff and volume driven operations costs, partly offset by lower \ntechnology costs. \nThe number of FTE increased by 28 or 2% on the prior half, from \n1,526 to 1,554 FTE, primarily driven by higher frontline and \nbusiness support resources. \nThe operating expenses to total operating income ratio increased \n250 basis points on the prior half to 44.7%, driven by lower \noperating income. \nLoan impairment expense was $33 million, an increase of \n$70 million on the prior half. This was driven by higher collective \nprovisions due to forward looking adjustments and the \nnon-recurrence of prior half provision releases, partly offset by \nhigher recoveries.  \nLoan impairment expense as a percentage of average gross \nloans and acceptances increased 15 basis points on the prior half \nto 0.07%. \nKey spot balance sheet movements included: \n\u2022 Interest earning lending assets balance decrease of $1.6 billion\nor 2%, primarily driven by a decrease in pooled facilities from\ngovernment sector clients utilising excess funds, and lower\nsecuritisation balances, partly offset by growth in the funds\nfinance and asset backed lending portfolios;\n\u2022 Non-lending interest earning assets decrease of $3.1 billion or\n4%, driven by lower reverse sale and repurchase agreement\nbalances in Markets, partly offset by an increase in the high\ngrade bond portfolio;\n\u2022 Other assets and non-interest bearing liabilities decrease of\n$9.4 billion or 30% and $7.4 billion or 29% respectively, mainly\ndriven by the revaluation of derivative assets and derivative\nliabilities due to foreign currency and interest rate movements,\npartly offset by timing of unsettled trades;\n\u2022 Total interest bearing deposits increase of $0.4 billion, mainly\ndriven by higher Transaction (including pooled facilities) and\nSavings deposits, partly offset by lower Investment deposits;\nand\n\u2022 Other interest bearing liabilities increase of $6.8 billion or 13%,\nmainly driven by an increase in sale and repurchase\nagreements in Markets.\nRisk weighted assets decreased $1.0 billion or 1% on the prior \nhalf, primarily driven by reduction in traded market risk weighted \nassets following the implementation of a new market risk engine \nand removal of the APRA RNIV capital overlay. \nInstitutional Banking and Markets generated $664 million of \norganic capital 1 for the Group in the current half. This contributed \n14 basis points to the Group\u2019s CET1 ratio.  \n1 \nOrganic capital generation represents cash net profit after tax less the \ncapital equivalent of the change in regulatory risk weighted assets \n(excluding impact of FX movements on Credit RWAs as they are capital \nneutral with offsetting impact in Foreign Currency Translation Reserves) \nused to generate those profits. The result was driven by a 5% decrease in total \noperating income, a 3% increase in operating expenses and a \n9% increase in loan impairment expense. \nNet interest income was NZD2,796 million, a decrease of \nNZD154 million or 5% on the prior year. This was driven by a 16 \nbasis point decrease in net interest margin, partly offset by a 2% \ngrowth in average interest earning assets. \nNet interest margin decreased 16 basis points, reflecting: \n\u2022 Lower deposit margins due to unfavourable mix as customers \nswitch to higher yielding products as well as lower term deposit \nmargins due to competition, partly offset by the benefit from the \nrising interest rate environment;  \n\u2022 Lower lending margins reflecting increased competition; and \n\u2022 Unfavourable asset mix from growth in liquid asset balances; \npartly offset by \n\u2022 Higher earnings on equity; and \n\u2022 Funding mix benefit driven by strong growth in deposits. \nOther operating income was NZD470 million, a decrease of \nNZD6 million or 1% on the prior year, reflecting: \n\u2022 Lower service fees due to fee removals and reductions on \nvarious accounts; and \n\u2022 Lower fair value gains and Markets earnings; partly offset by \n\u2022 Higher volume driven insurance income. \nOperating expenses were NZD1,299 million, an increase of \nNZD38 million or 3% on the prior year. The increase was \nprimarily driven by higher technology costs from increased \nsoftware licensing and amortisation, and higher staff costs from \nwage inflation. \nThe number of FTE decreased by 33 on the prior year from 6,016 \nto 5,983. \nInvestment spend continues to focus on regulatory compliance, \nsimplification and enhancing technology platforms.  \nThe operating expenses to total operating income ratio for ASB \nwas 39.8%, an increase of 300 basis points on the prior year \ndriven by lower operating income and higher operating \nexpenses.  \n \n \nLoan impairment expense was NZD70 million, an increase of \nNZD6 million or 9% on the prior year. This was mainly driven by \nhigher individually assessed provisions in the business portfolio \nand write-offs in the consumer finance portfolio, partly offset by \nlower \ncollective \nprovisions \npredominantly \nreflecting \nan \nimprovement in house price outlook compared to the prior year. \nHome loan 90+ days arrears increased 27 basis points to 0.61% \nand consumer finance 90+ days arrears increased 92 basis \npoints to 1.41%, due to increased cost of living pressures as well \nas delays in collections during the implementation of a new \nsystem.  \nKey spot balance sheet movements included: \n\u2022 Home loan growth of NZD0.5 billion or 1%, below system \ngrowth of 3% in a highly competitive environment; \n\u2022 Business and rural lending growth of NZD0.2 billion or 1%, \nbelow system growth; \n\u2022 Total customer deposit growth of NZD4.3 billion or 5% (interest \nbearing and non-interest bearing), above system growth 1 of \n4%, with greater customer demand for higher yielding deposits. \nRisk weighted assets were NZD71.4 billion, an increase of \nNZD0.6 billion or 1% on the prior year driven by an increase in \ncredit risk weighted assets and operational risk weighted assets \nfrom increased lending volumes, partly offset by lower market \nrisk weighted assets from reduced risk positions.  \nASB generated AUD1,517 million of organic capital 3 for the \nGroup in the current year. This contributed 27 basis points to the \nGroup's CET1 ratio. \n \n \n \n \n \n \n \n \n \n \n \n \n \n \n \n \n \n \n \n \n \n \n \n \n \n \n1 \nRBNZ system data includes institutional deposits which are excluded from \nthe ASB division Balance Sheet. \n2 \nRisk weighted assets reflect the New Zealand dollar amount calculated in \naccordance with RBNZ requirements.  \n3 \nOrganic capital generation represents cash net profit after tax less the \ncapital equivalent of the change in regulatory risk weighted assets \n(excluding impact of FX movements on Credit RWAs as they are capital \nneutral with offsetting impact in Foreign Currency Translation Reserves) \nused to generate those profits. \n  70 \n", "This page has been intentionally left blank \n", "71  \n   Commonwealth Bank of Australia \u2013 Profit Announcement \u2013 For the full year ended 30 June 2024 \nThe Group earns its returns from providing a broad range of banking products and services to retail and wholesale customers in Australia, \nNew Zealand and other jurisdictions.  \nLending and deposit taking are the Group\u2019s primary business activities with net interest income being the main contributor to the Group\u2019s \nresults. Net interest income is derived from the difference between interest earned on lending and investment assets and interest incurred \non customer deposits and wholesale debt raised to fund these assets. \nThe Group further generates income from lending fees and commissions, and trading activities. It also incurs costs associated with running \nthe business such as staff, occupancy and technology related expenses. \nThe Performance section provides details of the main contributors to the Group\u2019s returns and analysis of its financial performance by \nnature and geographical region. \nFull Year Ended \nHalf Year Ended \u00b9 \n30 Jun 24 \n30 Jun 23 \nJun 24 vs \n30 Jun 24 \n31 Dec Bank of Australia \u2013 Profit Announcement \u2013 For the full year ended 30 June 2024 \nInterest income and interest expense on financial assets and liabilities measured at amortised cost, and debt financial assets measured \nat fair value through OCI, are recognised using the effective interest method. Interest income recognition for these categories of financial \nassets depends on the expected credit losses (ECL) stage they are allocated to in accordance with the Group\u2019s ECL methodology. For \nfinancial assets classified within Stage 1 and Stage 2 interest income is calculated by applying the effective interest rate to the gross \ncarrying amount of the assets. Interest income on financial assets in Stage 3 is recognised by applying the effective interest rate to the \ngross carrying amount net of provisions for impairment. For details on the Group\u2019s ECL methodology refer to Note 3.2 of the 2024 Annual \nReport. \nFees, transaction costs and issue costs integral to financial assets and liabilities are capitalised and included in the interest recognised \nover the expected life of the instrument. This includes establishment fees for providing a loan or a lease arrangement. Facility and line \nfees in relation to commitments made under credit facilities where drawdown is assessed as probable are considered an integral part of \nthe effective interest rate and are recognised in net interest income. \nInterest income on finance leases is recognised progressively over the life of the lease, consistent with the outstanding investment and \nunearned income balance.  \nInterest income and expense on financial assets and liabilities that are classified at fair value through the Income Statement are accounted \nfor on a contractual rate basis and include amortisation of premiums/discounts.  \nInterest expense also includes payments made under a liquidity facility arrangement with the Reserve Bank of Australia, the Major Bank \nLevy (Bank Levy) expense and other financing charges. \n", "Commonwealth Bank of Australia \u2013 Profit Announcement \u2013 For the full year ended 30 June 2024  \n  73 \nFull Year Ended \nHalf Year Ended \u00b9 \n30 Jun 24 These financial assets \nare held within a business model whose objective is to hold financial assets in order to collect contractual cash flows. The contractual \ncash flows on these financial assets comprise the payment of principal and interest only. These instruments are measured at amortised \ncost.  \nLoans and other receivables, consistent with the Group\u2019s policy for all financial assets measured at amortised cost, are recognised on \nsettlement date, when funding is advanced to the borrowers. They are initially recognised at their fair value plus directly attributable \ntransaction costs such as broker fees and commissions. Subsequent to initial recognition, they are measured at amortised cost using the \neffective interest method and are presented net of provisions for impairment. The accounting policy for provisions for impairment is \nprovided in Appendix 2.2. For information on the Group\u2019s management of credit risk, refer to Note 9.2 of the 2024 Annual Report.  \nFinance leases, where the Group acts as lessor, are also included in Loans and other receivables. Finance leases are those where \nsubstantially all the risks and rewards of the lease asset have been transferred to the lessee. Lease receivables are recognised at an \namount equal to the net investment in the lease. Finance lease income reflects a constant periodic return on this net investment and is \nrecognised within Other interest income in the Income Statement.  \nWhen applying the effective interest method the Group has estimated the behavioural term of each loan portfolio by reference to historical \nprepayment rates and contractual maturities. \n", "Commonwealth Bank of Australia \u2013 Profit Announcement \u2013 For the full year ended 30 June 2024                    89 \nAs at 30 June 2024 \n \nHome \nLoans \n \nOther \nPersonal \u00b9 \nOther \nCommercial \nIndustrial \n \n \nTotal \n \n$M \n$M \n$M \n$M \nLoans which were past due but not impaired \u00b2 \n \n \n \n \nPast due 1 - While the Group\u2019s credit and responsible lending policies aim to minimise this risk, there will always \nbe instances where the Group will not receive the full amount owed and hence a provision for impaired loans will be necessary. \nA description of the key components of the Group\u2019s AASB 9 impairment methodology is provided in Note 3.2 of the 2024 Annual Report. \n", "92  \n   Commonwealth Bank of Australia \u2013 Profit Announcement \u2013 For the full year ended 30 June 2024 \nStable and well diversified funding sources are critical to the Group\u2019s ability to fund its lending and investing activities, and support growing \nits business.  \nOur main sources of funding include customer deposits, term funds raised in domestic and offshore wholesale markets via issuing debt \nsecurities and loan capital, and term funding from central banks. The Group also relies on repurchase agreements as a source of short-\nterm wholesale funding. \nComparative information has been revised to reflect the change detailed in Note 1.1 of the 2024 Annual Report. \n", "98  \n   Commonwealth Bank of Australia \u2013 Profit Announcement \u2013 For the full year ended 30 June 2024 \nShareholders\u2019 equity includes ordinary share capital, retained profits and reserves. Policies for each component are set out below: \nOrdinary shares are recognised at the amount paid up per ordinary share, net of directly attributable issue costs. Where the Bank or \nentities within the Group purchase shares in the Bank, the consideration paid is deducted from total shareholders\u2019 equity and the shares \nare treated as treasury shares until they are subsequently sold, reissued or cancelled. Where such shares are sold or reissued, any \nconsideration received is included in shareholders\u2019 equity. \nRetained profits includes the accumulated profits for the Group including certain amounts recognised directly in retained profits less \ndividends paid.  \nThe asset revaluation reserve is used to record revaluation adjustments on the Group\u2019s property assets. Where an asset is sold or \ndisposed of, any balance in the reserve in relation to the asset is transferred directly to retained profits. \nExchange differences arising on translation of the Group\u2019s foreign operations are accumulated in the foreign currency translation reserve. \nSpecifically, assets and liabilities are translated at the prevailing exchange rate at balance sheet date; revenue and expenses are \ntranslated at the transaction date; and all resulting exchange differences are recognised in the foreign currency translation reserve. \nWhen a foreign operation is disposed of, exchange differences are reclassified to the Income Statement. \nThe cash flow hedge reserve is used to record fair value gains or losses associated with the effective portion of designated cash flow \nhedging instruments. Amounts are reclassified to the Income Statement when the hedged transaction impacts profit or loss. \nEmployee compensation reserve is used to recognise the fair value of shares and other equity instruments issued to employees under \nthe employee share plans and bonus schemes. \nInvestment securities revaluation reserve includes changes in the fair value of investment securities measured at fair value through Other \nComprehensive Income. For debt securities, these changes are reclassified to the Income Statement when the asset is derecognised. \nFor equity securities, these changes are not reclassified to the Income Statement when derecognised. \n", "Commonwealth Bank of Australia \u2013 Profit Announcement \u2013 For the full year ended 30 June 2024                    99 \n \nFull Year Ended \n \nHalf Year Ended \n30 Jun 24 \n30 Jun 23  \n30 Jun 24 \n31 Dec 23 \nShares on Issue \nShares \nShares  \nShares \nShares \nOpening balance (excluding Treasury Shares deduction) \n1,676,169,322 1,701,538,406  1,674,651,934 1,676,169,322 \nShare buy-backs \n \n  \n \n \nOn-market buy-back \u00b9 \u00b2 \n(2,588,964) \n(25,369,084)  \n(1,071,576) \n(1,517,388) \nDividend reinvestment plan issues: \n \n  \n \n \n2021/2022 Final dividend fully paid ordinary shares $96.44 \u00b3 \n\u2013 \n\u2013  \n\u2013 \n\u2013 \n2022/2023 Interim dividend fully paid ordinary shares $97.37 \u00b3 \n\u2013 \n\u2013  \n\u2013 \n\u2013 \n2022/2023 Final dividend fully paid ordinary shares $101.10 \u00b3 \n\u2013 \n\u2013  \n\u2013 \n\u2013 \n2023/2024 Interim dividend fully paid ordinary shares $117.19 \u00b3 \n\u2013 \n\u2013  \n\u2013 \n\u2013 \nClosing balance (excluding Treasury Shares deduction) \n1,673,580,358 1,676,169,322  1,673,580,358 1,674,651,934 \nLess: Treasury Shares \u2074 \n(1,510,328) \n(1,649,931)  \n(1,510,328) \n(1,431,186) \nClosing balance \n1,672,070,030 1,674,519,391  1,672,070,030 1,673,220,748 \n1 \nOn 15 February 2023, the Group announced its intention to undertake an on-market share buy-back of up to $1 billion of CBA ordinary shares in addition to the \n$2 billion announcement on 9 February 2022. During the year ended 30 June 2023, the Group completed the $3 billion on-market buy-backs and bought back a \ntotal of 25,369,084 ordinary shares ($2,532 million) at an average price of $99.81. The shares bought back were subsequently cancelled. \n2 \nOn 9 August 2023, the Group announced its intention to conduct a further on-market share buy-back of up to $1 billion of CBA ordinary shares, with 2,588,964 \nordinary shares bought back at an average price of $108.84 ($282 million) during in the year ended 30 June 2024 (half year ended 30 June 2024: 1,071,576 ordinary \nshares bought back at an average price of $119.24 ($128 million); half year ended 31 December 2023: 1,517,388 ordinary shares bought back at $101.49 ($154 \nmillion)). The shares bought back were subsequently cancelled. \n3 \nThe DRP in respect of the interim 2023/2024, final 2022/2023, interim 2022/2023 and final 2021/2022 dividends were satisfied in full through the on-market purchase \nand transfer of 4,092,235 shares at $117.19, 7,183,122 shares at $101.10, 6,115,897 shares at $97.37 and 6,201,070 shares at $96.44, respectively, to participating \nshareholders. \n4 \nRelates to the movements in treasury shares held within the employee share scheme plans. \n  \nThe franking credits available to the Group at 30 June 2024, after \nallowing for Australian tax payable in respect of the current and \nprior reporting period\u2019s profit, are estimated  to be $1,861 million \n(31 December 2023: $1,688 million; 30 June 2023: $1,928 \nmillion). \nThe New Zealand imputation credits available to CBA at 30 June \n2024 are estimated to be NZ$894 million (31 December 2023: \nNZ$1,040 million; 30 June 2023: NZ$865 million). This is \ncalculated on the same basis as the Australian franking credits \nbut using the New Zealand current tax liability. \nThe Directors have determined a fully franked final dividend of \n250 cents per share amounting to $4,184 million. The dividend \nwill be payable on or around 27 September 2024 to shareholders \non the register at 5:00pm AEST on 22 August 2024. \nThe Board determines the dividend per share based on net profit \nafter tax (\u201ccash basis\u201d) per share, having regard to a range of \nfactors including: \n\u2022 Current and expected rates of business growth and the mix of \nbusiness; \n\u2022 Capital needs to support economic, regulatory and credit \nratings requirements; \n\u2022 Investments \nand/or \ndivestments \nto \nsupport \nbusiness \ndevelopment; \n\u2022 Competitors comparison and market expectations; and \n\u2022 Earnings per share growth. \nThe Group has a Dividend Reinvestment Plan (DRP) that is \navailable to shareholders in Australia and certain other \njurisdictions. Shareholders can elect to participate to acquire fully \npaid ordinary shares instead of receiving a cash dividend \npayment. Shares issued under DRP rank equally with ordinary \nshares on issue. The DRP for the 2024 interim dividend and 2023 \nfinal and interim dividends were satisfied in full by the on-market \npurchase and transfer of shares, and had participation rates of \n13.4%, 18.1% and 16.8%, respectively. \nThe register closes for determination of dividend entitlement at \n5:00pm AEST on 22 August 2024. The deadline for notifying a \nchange to participation in the DRP is 5:00pm AEST on 23 August \n2024. \nThe ex-dividend date is 21 August 2024. \n", "100  \n    Commonwealth Bank of Australia \u2013 Profit Announcement \u2013 For the full year ended 30 June 2024 \nThe Group is exposed to financial risks, non-financial risks and strategic risks arising from its operations. The Group manages these risks \nthrough its Risk Management Framework (the Framework), which evolves to accommodate changes in the business operating \nenvironment, better practice approaches, and regulatory and community expectations. The Group\u2019s key risk types are credit, market, \nliquidity, operational, compliance and strategic. The framework is discussed in Note 9.1 in the 2024 Annual Report.  \nThe Group\u2019s approach to risk management is described within Note 9 to the Financial Statements in the 2024 Annual Report. Further \ndisclosures in respect of capital adequacy and risk are provided in the Group\u2019s annual Pillar 3 document. \nThe Group uses a portfolio approach for the management of its credit risk, of which a key element is a well-diversified portfolio. drawings from the RBA TFF, RBNZ Funding for Lending Programme (FLP) and Term Lending Facility (TLF).  \n", "104                    Commonwealth Bank of Australia \u2013 Profit Announcement \u2013 For the full year ended 30 June 2024 \nThe Group\u2019s liquidity and funding policies are designed to \nensure it will meet its obligations as and when they fall due by \nensuring it is able to raise funding on an unsecured or secured \nbasis, has sufficient liquid assets to borrow against under \nrepurchase agreements or sell to raise immediate funds without \nadversely affecting the Group\u2019s net asset value.  \nThe Group\u2019s liquidity policies are designed to ensure it \nmaintains sufficient holdings of cash and liquid assets to meet \nits obligations to customers, in both ordinary market conditions \nand during periods of severe stress. These policies are intended \nto protect the value of the Group\u2019s operations during periods of \nunfavourable market conditions.  \nThe Group\u2019s funding policies are designed to achieve diversified \nsources of funding by product, term, maturity date, investor type, \ninvestor location, currency and concentration, on a cost effective \nbasis. This objective applies to the Group\u2019s wholesale and retail \nfunding activities.  \nThe CBA Board is responsible for the sound and prudent \nmanagement of liquidity risk across the Group. The Group\u2019s \nliquidity and funding policies, structured under the Group \nLiquidity Risk Management Framework, are approved by the \nBoard. The Group Asset and Liability Committee\u2019s (ALCO) \nresponsibilities include asset and liability management, \nreviewing liquidity and funding policies and strategies, and \nmonitoring compliance with those policies across the Group. \nGroup Treasury manages the Group\u2019s liquidity and funding \npositions in accordance with the Group\u2019s Liquidity Policy and \nsupporting standards, and has ultimate authority to execute \nliquidity and funding decisions should the Group Contingency \nFunding Plan be activated. Risk Management provides \noversight of the Group\u2019s liquidity and funding risks, compliance \nwith Group policies and manages the Group\u2019s relationship with \nprudential regulators.  \nSubsidiaries within the Group apply their own liquidity and \nfunding strategies to address their specific needs. The Group\u2019s \nNew Zealand banking subsidiary, ASB, manages its own \ndomestic liquidity and funding needs in accordance with its own \nliquidity policy and the policies of the Group. ASB\u2019s liquidity \npolicy is also overseen by the RBNZ.  \nThe Group\u2019s liquidity and funding policies provide that: \n\u2022 an excess of liquid assets over the minimum prescribed under \nAPRA\u2019s Liquidity Coverage Ratio (LCR) requirement is \nmaintained. Australian ADIs are required to meet a 100% \nLCR, calculated as the ratio of high quality liquid assets to 30 \nday net cash outflows projected under a prescribed stress \nscenario;  \n\u2022 a surplus of stable funding from various sources, as measured \nby APRA\u2019s Net Stable Funding Ratio (NSFR), is maintained. \nThe NSFR is calculated by applying factors prescribed by \nAPRA to assets and liabilities to determine a ratio of required \nstable funding to available stable funding which must be \ngreater than 100%; \n\u2022 scenario analysis is central to the Group\u2019s liquidity \nmanagement framework and the Group undertakes additional \nstress testing including market specific and idiosyncratic \nscenarios over and above the regulatory defined scenarios; \n\u2022 additional funding and liquidity metrics are calculated and \nmonitored as early warning indicators of a potential stress \nevent;  \n\u2022 short and long-term wholesale funding limits are established, \nmonitored and reviewed regularly;  \n\u2022 the Group\u2019s wholesale funding market capacity is regularly \nassessed and used as a factor in funding strategies; \n\u2022 Group Treasury maintains a portfolio of highly liquid assets to \nmeet liquidity requirements under a range of market \nconditions. The liquid asset portfolio includes cash and liquid \nassets, \nincluding \ngovernment \nand \nAustralian \nsemi-\ngovernment securities, meeting APRA\u2019s High Quality Liquid \nAsset (HQLA) definition and other highly liquid assets which \nare repo-eligible with the Reserve Bank of Australia (RBA); \n\u2022 liquid assets are held in Australian dollar and foreign currency \ndenominated securities \nin \naccordance \nwith \nexpected \nrequirements;  \n\u2022 in line with APRA\u2019s requirements to hold adequate levels of \nself-securitised assets, the Group also holds internal RMBS \n(minimum value of 30% of Group net cash outflows as defined \nunder the LCR), which are mortgages that have been \nsecuritised but retained by the Bank, that are repo-eligible with \nthe RBA under the Exceptional Liquidity Assistance (ELA) \narrangement; and \n\u2022 offshore branches and subsidiaries adhere to liquidity policies \nand hold appropriate foreign currency liquid assets to meet \nrequired regulations. Material banking subsidiaries are \nrequired to maintain an LCR of at least 100%. \nThe Group\u2019s key funding tools include: \n\u2022 consumer retail funding base, which includes a wide range of \nretail transaction accounts, savings accounts and term \ndeposits for individual consumers;  \n\u2022 small business customer and institutional deposit base; and \n\u2022 wholesale domestic and international funding programmes, \nwhich include Australian dollar Negotiable Certificates of \nDeposit, US and Euro Commercial Paper programmes, \nAustralian dollar Domestic Debt Programme, US Medium-\nTerm \nNote \nProgrammes, \nEuro \nMedium-Term \nNote \nProgramme, multi-jurisdiction Covered Bond programmes and \nMedallion securitisation programmes. Additionally the Group \nhas accessed the RBA\u2019s Term Funding Facility1 (TFF) and \nRBNZ term lending facilities. \nLiquidity modelling and forecasting is undertaken on a daily \nbasis to ensure the Group meets its internal and regulatory \nliquidity requirements at all times. A regulatory liquidity \nmanagement reporting system models and reports regulatory \nliquidity outcomes. Additionally a comprehensive Funds \nTransfer Pricing framework is in place to attribute the cost of \nfunding and liquidity to business units and to provide appropriate \nincentives to inform business decision making. \nThe Group maintains a Contingency Funding Plan (CFP) which \ndetails how the Group would respond to a liquidity stress event. \nThe plan includes details of roles and responsibilities including \nthe committee of responsible executives, early warning \nindicators and trigger events, potential contingent funding \nactions that could be undertaken to manage the Group\u2019s liquidity \nposition as well as a communications strategy. The plan is \nregularly tested and is approved by the Board on an annual \nbasis. \n1 \nThe TFF has subsequently been fully repaid.\n", "Commonwealth Bank of Australia \u2013 Profit Announcement \u2013 For the full year ended 30 June 2024  \n  105 \nThe Group provides leveraged finance to companies. The loss includes a $133 million impairment loss \non remeasurement of PTBC\u2019s net assets to fair value, an \nadditional $100 million loss recognised upon the completion of \nthe sale, and $65 million of separation costs. \nOn 21 June 2021, the Group announced the sale of CommInsure \nGeneral Insurance to Hollard Insurance Company Pty Ltd \n(Hollard). As part of the sale, the Group established an exclusive \n15-year strategic alliance with Hollard for the distribution of home \nand motor vehicle insurance products. The sale of CommInsure \nGeneral Insurance to Hollard completed on 30 September 2022, \nresulting in a total post-tax gain of $66 million net of transaction \nand separation costs. This includes a $179 million post-tax gain \nrecognised during the year ended 30 June 2023, and post-tax \ntransaction and separation costs of $46 million and $67 million \nrecognised during the years ended 30 June 2022 and 2021, \nrespectively. \nPTBC and CommInsure General Insurance did not represent \nseparate major lines of the Group\u2019s business and were not \nclassified as discontinued operations. \nProvisions for customer remediation require significant levels of \nestimation and judgement. The amount raised depends on a \nnumber of different assumptions, such as the number of years \nimpacted, the forecast remediation fund rate and the average \ncost per case. The Group is committed to comprehensively and \nefficiently addressing the full range of remediation issues \nimpacting customers of the Banking and former Wealth \nManagement businesses. Significant resources have been \ncommitted to a comprehensive program of work, to ensure that \nissues are identified and addressed. \nAligned advisors were not employed by the Group but were \nrepresentatives authorised to provide financial advice under the \nlicences of the Group\u2019s subsidiaries, Financial Wisdom Limited \n(FWL), Count Financial Limited (Count Financial) and \nCommonwealth Financial Planning Limited-Pathways (CFP-\nPathways). The Group completed the sale of Count Financial to \nCount Limited (Count) on 1 October 2019, and ceased providing \nlicensee services through CFP-Pathways and Financial Wisdom \nin March and June 2020, respectively. The Bank entered into \nreimbursement agreements with Financial Wisdom and CFP-\nPathways, and an indemnity deed with Count to cover potential \nremediation of past issues including ongoing service fees and \ncommissions, and other remediation matters. For details on the \nreimbursement agreements and the indemnity deed, refer to \nNote 11.2 in the 2024 Annual Report. \nDuring the year ended 30 June 2024, the Group recognised an \nincrease in the provision for Aligned Advice remediation issues \nand program costs of $7 million. In addition, the Group paid $137 \nmillion in customer refunds for ongoing service fees, $63 million \nin other remediation matters and utilised $29 million for program \ncosts. \nAs at 30 June 2024, the Group holds a provision of $40 million \n(30 June 2023: $262 million). The Group has made all customer \nrefunds in relation to ongoing service fees remediation, and \ncontinues to engage with ASIC in relation to remediation \nprograms. \n \n  \n", "110                    Commonwealth Bank of Australia \u2013 Profit Announcement \u2013 For the full year ended 30 June 2024 \nAs at 30 June 2024, the provision held by the Group in relation \nto Banking customer remediation programs was $173 million (30 \nJune 2023: $84 million). The provision includes an estimate of \ncustomer refunds (including interest) relating to business and \nretail banking products and the related program costs. \nThe Group is party to a number of legal proceedings, and the \nsubject of various investigations and reviews. Provisions have \nbeen raised in accordance with the principles outlined in the \naccounting policy section of this note.  \nThe main litigated claims against the Group as at 30 June 2024 \nare summarised below. \nIn October 2017 and June 2018, two separate shareholder class \naction proceedings were filed against CBA in the Federal Court \nof Australia, alleging breaches of CBA\u2019s continuous disclosure \nobligations and misleading and deceptive conduct in relation to \nthe subject matter of the civil penalty proceedings brought \nagainst CBA by the Australian Transaction Reports and Analysis \nCentre (AUSTRAC). The AUSTRAC proceedings concerned \ncontraventions of the Anti-Money Laundering and Counter-\nTerrorism Financing Act 2006 (Cth). \nThe resolution of the AUSTRAC civil penalty proceedings was \napproved by the Federal Court on 20 June 2018 with CBA paying \na penalty of $700 million and legal costs. It was alleged in the \nclass actions that CBA shareholders who acquired an interest in \nCBA shares between 16 June 2014 and 3 August 2017 suffered \nlosses as a result of the alleged conduct. The two class actions \nwere being case managed together, with a single harmonised \nstatement of claim. On 10 May 2024, the Federal Court handed \ndown judgment in CBA\u2019s favour and on 28 May 2024 orders were \nmade dismissing both class actions. The Applicants filed an \nappeal from the judgement on 25 June 2024. CBA is defending \nthe appeal. It is currently not possible to determine the ultimate \nimpact of this claim, if any, on the Group. \nThe Group is also defending three class actions in relation to \nsuperannuation products.  \nOn 9 October 2018, a class action was filed against Colonial First \nState Investments Limited (CFSIL) and CBA in the Federal Court \nof Australia. The claim initially related to investment in cash and \ndeposit options (which are cash and deposit products provided \nby CBA) in the Colonial First State First Choice Superannuation \nTrust (FirstChoice Fund) and Commonwealth Essential Super \nand later expanded to join Avanteos Investments Limited (AIL) \nas a party in respect of claims regarding the FirstWrap Pooled \nCash Account. \nThe main claims are that members who invested in these cash \nand deposit options received lower interest rates than they could \nhave received had CFSIL/AIL offered similar products made \navailable in the market by another bank with comparable risk and \nthat CFSIL/AIL retained the margin that arises through the \ninternal transfer pricing process in respect of deposits made with \nCBA, for their own benefit. It is claimed CFSIL/AIL breached their \nduties as a trustee of the funds, CFSIL breached its duties as a \nResponsible Entity of the underlying managed investment \nschemes and that CBA was involved in CFSIL/AIL\u2019s breaches. \nCBA, CFSIL and AIL deny the allegations and are defending the \nproceedings.  \nOn 18 October 2019, a second class action was commenced \nagainst CFSIL in the Federal Court of Australia. The claim related \nto certain fees charged to members of the FirstChoice Fund. It \nalleged that CFSIL breached its duties as trustee and acted \nunconscionably because it failed, between 2013 and 2019, to \ntake steps to avoid the payment of grandfathered commissions \nto financial advisers, which would have resulted in a reduction of \nthe fees paid by members in respect of whom those commissions \nwere paid. CFSIL denied the allegations and defended the \nproceedings. Following a mediation in June 2023, a settlement \nwas reached with no admissions as to liability. On 5 August 2024, \nthe Court approved the settlement. \nOn 22 January 2020, a further class action was filed against \nCFSIL and The Colonial Mutual Life Assurance Society Limited \n(CMLA) in the Federal Court of Australia. On 22 October 2021, \nAIA Australia Limited (AIAA), who from 1 April 2021 was liable \nfor and assumed certain liabilities of CMLA under a life insurance \nscheme pursuant to Part 9 of the Life Insurance Act 1995 (Cth) \n(Part 9 Scheme), was joined as a third respondent to the class \naction. The class action alleges that CFSIL did not act in the best \ninterests of members and breached its trustee duties when taking \nout group insurance policies obtained from CMLA. The key \nallegation is that CFSIL entered into and maintained insurance \npolicies with CMLA on terms that were less favourable to \nmembers than would have reasonably been available in the \nmarket. It is alleged that CMLA was knowingly involved in \nCFSIL\u2019s contraventions as trustee and profited from those \ncontraventions. CFSIL, CMLA and AIAA deny the allegations and \nare defending the proceedings. A mediation took place in \nDecember 2023 which did not result in an agreement being \nreached, and it is anticipated a further mediation will take place \nin December 2024. The class action has been provisionally listed \nfor a three week trial commencing 4 August 2025. \nOn 1 December 2021, the Group completed the sale of a 55% \ninterest in Colonial First State (CFS) to KKR. CBA has assumed \ncarriage of the superannuation class actions proceedings on \nCFSIL\u2019s and AIL\u2019s behalf subject to the terms of a conduct \nindemnity deed between CBA, CFSIL and AIL. The Group has \nprovided for certain legal and other costs associated with its \nobligations under the indemnity deed. \nOn 21 August 2020, a class action was filed in the Federal Court \nof Australia against Commonwealth Financial Planning Limited \n(CFP), FWL and CMLA. The claim relates to certain CommInsure \n(CMLA) life insurance policies recommended by financial \nadvisers appointed by CFP and FWL during the period from 21 \nAugust 2014 to 21 August 2020. On 16 November 2021, AIAA \n(who from 1 April 2021 was liable for and assumed certain \nliabilities of CMLA under the Part 9 Scheme) was joined as a \nfourth respondent to the class action.  The key allegations include \nthat CFP and FWL or their financial advisers breached their \nfiduciary duties to their clients, breached their duty to act in the \nbest interest of their clients, and had prioritised their own \ninterests (and the interests of CFP, FWL and CMLA) over the \ninterest of their clients, in recommending certain CMLA life \ninsurance policies in preference to substantially equivalent or \nbetter policies available at lower premiums from third party \ninsurers. It is also alleged that CMLA knew the material facts \ngiving rise to the breaches of fiduciary duty. CFP, FWL, CMLA \nand AIAA deny the allegations and are defending the \nproceedings. It is currently not possible to determine the ultimate \nimpact of this claim, if any, on the Group. \n", "Commonwealth Bank of Australia \u2013 Profit Announcement \u2013 For the full year ended 30 June 2024                    111 \nOn 24 August 2020 a class action was commenced against \nCount Financial in the Federal Court of Australia. The proceeding \nrelates to commissions paid to Count Financial and its authorised \nrepresentative financial advisers in respect of financial products \n(including insurance) and certain obligations of its financial \nadvisers to provide ongoing advice in the period from 21 August \n2014 to 21 August 2020. The claim also includes allegations \n(related to the receipt of commissions) that Count Financial \nengaged in misleading or deceptive conduct, and that Count \nFinancial and its authorised representatives breached fiduciary \nduties owed to the applicant and group members. The claim \nseeks compensation and damages from Count Financial, \nincluding any profits resulting from the alleged contraventions.  A \npre-trial mediation did not resolve the class action and the matter \nproceeded to a 3 week initial trial in March 2024. Judgement is \nreserved. \nCount Financial was a wholly owned subsidiary of CBA until 1 \nOctober 2019, when it was acquired by Count Limited. CBA has \nassumed the conduct of the defence in this matter on Count \nFinancial\u2019s behalf. Count Financial denies the allegations made \nagainst it and defended the proceedings. The Group has \nprovided for certain legal and other costs associated with any \nindemnity obligations. \nOn 10 June 2020, a class action was commenced against CBA \nand CMLA in the Federal Court of Australia. The claim related to \nconsumer credit insurance for credit cards and personal loans \nthat was sold between 1 January 2010 and 7 March 2018. On 1 \nApril 2022, AIAA (who from 1 April 2021 was liable for and \nassumed certain liabilities of CMLA under the Part 9 Scheme) \nwas joined as a third respondent to the class action. The class \naction alleged that CBA and CMLA engaged in unconscionable \nand misleading or deceptive conduct, failed to act in the best \ninterests of customers and provided them with inappropriate \nadvice. In particular, it was alleged that some customers were \nexcluded from claiming certain benefits under the policies and \nthe insurance was therefore unsuitable or of no value. Allegations \nwere also made in relation to the manner in which the insurance \nwas sold. CBA, CMLA and AIAA denied the allegations. \nOn 18 October 2022, the parties attended a Court ordered \nmediation following which they entered into a settlement \nagreement to resolve the proceedings. The settlement was made \nwithout admission of liability. On 15 September 2023, the Court \napproved the settlement. The Court has ordered that the case be \ndismissed once the settlement distribution process has been \ncompleted. \n \nProceedings were served on CBA subsidiary ASB Bank Limited \n(ASB) on 29 September 2021 by plaintiffs seeking to bring a \nrepresentative (class action) proceeding against ASB in the High \nCourt of New Zealand. These proceedings relate to ASB\u2019s \ncompliance with parts of the Credit Contracts and Consumer \nFinance Act 2003 (NZ) (CCCFA) which requires a variation \ndisclosure to be issued when customers and ASB make agreed \nchanges to loan agreements captured under the CCCFA. \nOn 23 and 24 April 2024, the New Zealand Court of Appeal heard \nASB\u2019s appeal from an earlier High Court decision permitting the \nplaintiffs to pursue their claims as an opt-out representative \nproceeding on behalf of a class. On 19 July 2024, the Court of \nAppeal confirmed the earlier Court\u2019s decision to allow the \nplaintiffs to bring the action against ASB as an opt-out \nrepresentative action. \nThe parties have until 16 August 2024 to apply to the Supreme \nCourt of New Zealand for permission to appeal against the Court \nof Appeal\u2019s decision. \nThe plaintiffs' proposed class definition covers customers who \nhad a home or personal loan with ASB between 6 June 2015 and \n18 June 2019 covered by the CCCFA and who were not provided \nwith compliant variation disclosure. Given this definition and the \nfact that issues raised in the claim have not been determined by \nthe Courts before, the size of the proposed class is unknown. \nHowever, the proposed class and the allegations made in the \nproceedings would potentially cover hundreds of thousands of \nloans. \nIn their claim, the plaintiffs argue that ASB is not entitled to retain \nany interest or fees paid by any class member for the period \nduring which it is alleged that ASB did not provide, and has not \nprovided, compliant variation disclosure under the CCCFA. ASB \ndenies that the relief sought by the plaintiffs is available to them \nand is vigorously defending the proceedings. \nIt is not possible to determine the ultimate impact of this claim, if \nany, on the Group. \nIn October 2021, the Fair Work Ombudsman (FWO) commenced \ncivil penalty proceedings in the Federal Court of Australia against \nCBA and CommSec, alleging contraventions of the Fair Work Act \n2009 (Cth) (Fair Work Act), and of the Group\u2019s 2014 and 2016 \nenterprise \nagreements. \nThe \nproceedings \nfollowed \nan \ninvestigation by the FWO of the Group\u2019s employee entitlement \nreview (EER). CBA self-disclosed these matters in the EER to \nthe FWO.  \nCBA and CommSec cooperated fully with the FWO and agreed \na statement of agreed facts and admissions with the FWO. A \nhearing to determine penalty was held in September 2023. On \n15 February 2024, the Federal Court handed down judgment and \nordered CBA to pay a penalty of $7.31 million and CommSec to \npay a penalty of $3.03 million. The penalties have been paid. \nCBA\u2019s broad remediation review of employee entitlements for \ncurrent and former employees is complete. \n \n", "112  \n    Commonwealth Bank of Australia \u2013 Profit Announcement \u2013 For the full year ended 30 June 2024 \nIn August 2022, the Wage Inspectorate Victoria commenced \ncriminal proceedings against each of CommSec and BWA Group \nServices Pty Ltd (BWA) in the Magistrates\u2019 Court of Victoria. The \nproceedings relate to alleged underpayments of approximately \n$60,000 in long service leave (LSL) entitlements for 17 former \nemployees of those entities (8 employees of CommSec and 9 \nemployees of BWA). LSL underpayments are included in the \nGroup\u2019s EER described above. \nA Plea Hearing was held on 29 July 2024 in the Magistrates\u2019 \nCourt of Victoria. The Court imposed a penalty of $18,000 for \nCommSec and $18,000 for BWA. No conviction was recorded for \neither entity. The Court also made an order for the Wage \nInspectorate Victoria\u2019s costs to be paid by CommSec and BWA, \nfixed at $12,000, as agreed by the parties.  \nThe Group undertakes ongoing compliance activities, including \nbreach reporting, reviews of products, advice, conduct and \nservices provided to customers, as well as interest, fees and \npremiums charged. Some of these activities have resulted in \nremediation programs and where required the Group consults \nwith the relevant regulator and other bodies on the proposed \nremediation action.  \nProvisions have been recognised by the Group where the criteria \noutlined in the accounting policy section of this note are satisfied. \nContingent liabilities exist with respect to these matters where it \nis not possible to determine the extent of any obligation to \nremediate or the potential liability cannot be reliably estimated. \nThere are also ongoing matters where regulators or other bodies \nare investigating whether CBA, ASB or another Group entity has \nbreached laws, regulatory or other obligations. Where a breach \nhas occurred, or obligations have not been met, regulators or \nother bodies may impose, or apply to a Court for, fines and/or \nother sanctions or may require remediation. These matters \ninclude investigations of a number of issues which were notified \nto, or identified by, regulators or other bodies. \nIn addition to possible regulatory actions and reviews, there may \nalso be financial exposure to claims by customers, third parties \nand shareholders and this could include further class actions, \ncustomer remediation or claims for compensation or other \nremedies. The outcomes and total costs associated with such \nregulatory actions and reviews, and possible claims remain \nuncertain. \nThe following matters were significant regulatory investigations \nand reviews, which have been completed, but have resulted in \nongoing action required by the Group. \nAs noted above, in 2018 the Group resolved the AUSTRAC \nproceedings \nrelating \nto \ncontraventions \nof \nanti-money \nlaundering/counter-terrorism financing (AML/CTF) laws. CBA \ncontinues to address the underlying causes of the Anti-Money \nLaundering and Counter-Terrorism Financing Act 2006 (Cth) \n(AML/CTF Act) failings that resulted in AUSTRAC commencing \nits proceedings. \nRecognising the crucial role that the Group plays in fighting \nfinancial crime, it continues to invest significantly in its financial \ncrime disruption capabilities, including in its central AML/CTF \nCompliance team, its business unit-led risk teams, regulatory \nand control operations team and through the Program of Action, \nwith coverage across financial crime (including AML/CTF, \nsanctions, anti-bribery and corruption and anti-tax evasion \nfacilitation). \nWe also continue to invest in people, systems, processes and \ncontrols to respond to rapidly evolving regulatory environments, \ndevelopments in financial crime and other changes in the \nlandscape in which we operate, such as the increasingly \nsophisticated use of technology by criminals targeting the \nfinancial system, and the increase of scams, fraud, ransomware \nand cyber-attacks. \nThe Group continues to review and remediate a number of \nknown AML/CTF compliance issues. As this work progresses, \nfurther compliance issues may be identified and reported to \nAUSTRAC or other regulators, and additional enhancements of \nsystems and processes may be required. \nThe Group provides updates to AUSTRAC and other regulators \non its Anti-Money Laundering and Counter-Terrorism Financing \nProgram and other financial crime compliance capabilities, \nrelated enhancements and remediation activities. \nHowever, there is no assurance that AUSTRAC or other \nregulators will agree that the Group\u2019s enhancements to its \nfinancial crime compliance capabilities, including through the \nmulti-year Program of Action, are adequate or will effectively \nenhance the Group\u2019s financial crime compliance programs \nacross its business units and the jurisdictions in which it \noperates. There is also a risk of undetected failure of internal \ncontrols, or the ineffective remediation of compliance issues \nwhich could lead to breaches of AML/CTF, sanctions, anti-\nbribery and corruption and anti-tax evasion facilitation \nobligations, resulting in potentially significant monetary and \nregulatory penalties. \nAlthough the Group is not currently aware of any enforcement \nproceeding being commenced by any domestic or foreign \nregulators in respect of its financial crime compliance, the Group \nregularly engages with such regulators, including in respect of \ncompliance issues, and there can be no assurance that the \nGroup will not be subject to such enforcement proceedings in the \nfuture. \nIn June 2019, the Australian Information and Privacy \nCommissioner (Commissioner) accepted an EU offered by CBA, \nwhich required further enhancements to the management and \nretention of customer personal information within CBA and \ncertain subsidiaries. CBA completed the formal obligations under \nthe EU during the year ended 30 June 2024. \nAs part of the proceedings ASIC commenced against CommSec \nin October 2022, the Federal Court ordered CommSec to \nundertake a compliance program. As required by the program, \nCommSec has appointed an independent expert to review the \nadequacy and effectiveness of its remediation of the issues in the \nproceedings and their root causes, as well as the adequacy of its \nsystems and controls. The independent expert has prepared an \ninitial report and CommSec has agreed a remedial action plan \nwith ASIC, to address the recommendations made in the report. \nThe independent expert will conduct a final review once all the \nactions from the remedial action plan have been implemented.  \n", "Commonwealth Bank of Australia \u2013 Profit Announcement \u2013 For the full year ended 30 June 2024  \n  113 \nIn connection with breaches of certain provisions of the Spam \nAct 2003 (Cth) (Spam Act), CBA has paid the ACMA a fine of \n$3.55 million and on 2 June 2023 entered into an EU with the \nACMA. As required by the EU, CBA has appointed an \nindependent consultant to review its current procedures, policies, \ntraining and systems relating to CBA\u2019s compliance with the Spam \nAct. CBA has provided the ACMA with its plan to implement the \nindependent consultant\u2019s recommendations, and has committed \nto providing ongoing compliance reports to the ACMA and \ntraining relevant personnel under the EU. The independent \nconsultant has provided its initial report under the EU, and will \nconduct further reviews, as set out in the EU, or as otherwise \nrequired. CBA continues to review its compliance with the Spam \nAct and it considers that further rectification steps will be \nrequired.  \nThe Group has potential exposures to divested businesses, \nincluding through the provision of services, warranties and \nindemnities. These exposures may have an adverse impact on \nthe Group\u2019s financial performance and position. The Group has \nrecognised provisions where payments in relation to the \nexposures are probable and reliably measurable. \nNot applicable. \nThis preliminary final report for the year ended 30 June 2024 is \nprepared in accordance with the ASX listing rules. It should be \nread in conjunction with any announcements to the market made \nby the Group during the year. PricewaterhouseCoopers has \naudited \nthe \nfinancial \nstatements \ncontained \nwithin \nthe \nCommonwealth Bank of Australia Annual Report and has issued \nan unmodified audit report. The Annual Report has been \npublished together with the preliminary report. This preliminary \nfinal \nreport \nhas \nnot \nbeen \nsubject \nto \naudit \nby \nPricewaterhouseCoopers. The preceding financial information \ncontained in the Financial Statements section of this preliminary \nfinal report includes financial information extracted from the \naudited financial statements together with financial information \nthat has not been audited. \n", "114  \n    Commonwealth Bank of Australia \u2013 Profit Announcement \u2013 For the full year ended 30 June 2024 \nNon-cash items are excluded from net profit after tax (\u201ccash basis\u201d), which is management\u2019s preferred measure of the Group\u2019s financial \nperformance, as they tend to be non-recurring in nature or are not considered representative of the Group\u2019s ongoing financial performance. \nThe impact of these items on the Group\u2019s net profit after tax (\u201cstatutory basis\u201d) is outlined below and treated consistently with the prior \nfinancial year. This is measured from two perspectives: firstly by quantifying the change in the net present \nvalue of the Balance Sheet\u2019s future earnings potential, and secondly as the anticipated change to Net \nInterest Income earned over 12 months. ASF is the portion of \nan Authorised Deposit-taking Institution\u2019s (ADI) capital and liabilities expected to be a reliable source of \nfunds over a one year time horizon. def build_attribution(payload: dict, research: Research, case: dict, metric_cfg: dict,

    the artifact stays one contract rather than two.

        movement.get(k) is None for k in ("from_value", "to_value", "delta")
    ):
        movement = None
        reply.setdefault("limitations", []).append(
            "The movement could not be established from the evidence."
        )
    if isinstance(movement, dict) and metric_cfg["unit"] == "bps":
        frm, to = movement.get("from_value"), movement.get("to_value")
        if (
            isinstance(frm, (int, float))
            and isinstance(to, (int, float))
            and max(abs(frm), abs(to)) < 100
            and _percent_evidenced(frm, records)
            and _percent_evidenced(to, records)
        ):
            movement["from_value"], movement["to_value"] = frm * 100, to * 100
            if abs(movement.get("delta", 0) - round((to - frm) * 100, 1)) > (
                movement_arithmetic_tolerance(movement.get("unit"))
            ):
                movement["delta"] = round((to - frm) * 100, 1)
            reply.setdefault("limitations", []).append(
                f"Movement endpoints converted from percent ({frm}, {to}) to bps: the unit "
                "for this metric is bps."
            )
    if isinstance(movement, dict):
        movement = settle_charge_sign(movement, metric_cfg, reply)
    if isinstance(movement, dict):
        # The threshold is check_movement's own, indexed by the movement's unit
        # (author.py carries the same repair and the same reason).
        implied = round(movement["to_value"] - movement["from_value"], 2)
        if (
            abs(movement["delta"] - implied)
            > movement_arithmetic_tolerance(movement.get("unit"))
            and implied != 0

                "(unit slip against the endpoints)."

def _keep_valid(items, model, dropped: list[str], what: str) -> list:
    """Every item the schema accepts, with each rejection recorded.

    One malformed sub-object must not cost a whole research run its answer. A
    driver rated 105, or a disagreement whose reason is not one of the five,
    is dropped and named in limitations — the artifact then says what it lost,
    which is the honest outcome and the one a reader can check.
    """
    kept = []
    for item in items or []:
        try:
            kept.append(model.model_validate(item))
        except Exception as exc:  # noqa: BLE001
            dropped.append(f"{what} dropped as malformed ({str(exc).splitlines()[0][:120]})")
    return kept


def _snippet(text: str, query: str) -> str:
    """A window of the page around the first query word that appears on it."""
    words = [w for w in re.findall(r"[A-Za-z]{4,}", query.lower())]
    lowered = text.lower()
    at = next((lowered.find(w) for w in words if lowered.find(w) >= 0), -1)
    start = max(0, at - SNIPPET_CHARS // 3) if at >= 0 else 0
    return re.sub(r"\s+", " ", text[start:start + SNIPPET_CHARS]).strip()

  1117	def _quote_numbers(quote: str | None) -> list[tuple[float, str]]:
  1118	    """(magnitude, unit) for every number a verbatim quote states.

  1121	    number bare. The caller decides what a bare number may ground.

  1126	            value = abs(float(token.replace(",", "")))
  1127	        except ValueError:  # pragma: no cover - the pattern admits only numbers
  1128	            continue

  1130	        # PDF text layer breaks a line wherever it likes.

  1133	            not unit

  1135	            and "." not in token

  1144	def _converted_prints(quoted: float, quoted_unit: str, value: float, unit: str | None) -> bool:
  1145	    """Does a number the quote printed in ONE unit state this claim in another?
  1146	
  1147	    The slack is the TIGHTER of the two units' own slack, both read in the
  1148	    claim's unit. A single tolerance taken from the claim's unit is wrong in
  1149	    both directions once a conversion sits between the two numbers: the
  1150	    citation slack for ppt is 0.1, which is TEN BASIS POINTS, so the sentence
  1151	    "Return on equity increased 10 basis points" grounded a component claim of
  1152	    +0.08 ppt and of +0.02 ppt at once — the whole movement was inside the
  1153	    slack. Read the other way, a "$2.5bn" quote carries 0.5 $bn of slack, which
  1154	    is $500m against a $m claim.

  1156	    A page prints a number to its own unit's precision, and a claim is stated
  1157	    to its own. Neither may be relaxed by the conversion between them.

  1163	    quoted_tol = convert_unit(
  1164	        _tolerance_for(CITATION_TOL, quoted_unit, CITATION_TOL_DEFAULT), quoted_unit, unit
  1165	    )
  1166	    tolerance = claim_tol if quoted_tol is None else min(claim_tol, quoted_tol)

   202	def _numbers_the_quote_prints(quote: str, raw_numbers) -> list[NumberFact]:
   203	    """The NumberFacts of one record, minus the ones its own quote contradicts.
   204	
   205	    A NumberFact is the model's own account of what the quote states, and this
   206	    stage took it on trust: an extractor could pair a real verbatim sentence
   207	    with a figure of its own, and every check that reads record.numbers — the
   208	    column checks, the percent-evidence tests, the citation cap — would then
   209	    read a number no page prints. The agent shell verifies the same thing at
   210	    its own mint point (research_agent._mint_record), from the same function.
   211	
   212	    The gate is narrower here than there, and measurement is why. The agent's
   213	    `cite` verifies the quote against the PAGE first and hands every drop back
   214	    to the model, which re-quotes. This stage does neither, and its quote is
   215	    often a row LABEL with the row's figures in `numbers`: applied at full
   216	    strength the gate dropped 18.6% of the shipped facts, and the WBC FY25 ROE
   217	    case lost its movement outright because all six of its records quoted a
   218	    label ("ROTE", "Average ordinary equity ($m)").
   219	
   220	    So a quote that prints NO number says nothing about the numbers beside it,
   221	    and they are kept — absence of evidence is not a conflict. A quote that
   222	    DOES print numbers is the model quoting the row, and a fact that row does
   223	    not carry is the model's own arithmetic or another row's column: "Loan
   224	    impairment expense was $554 million, a decrease of $1,964 million" carried
   225	    a fact of 2,518, and "Treasury & Markets impact on NIM 0.13% 0.13%"
   226	    carried a fact of 0 bps. Those are dropped.
   227	    """
   228	    facts: list[NumberFact] = []
   229	    for number in raw_numbers if isinstance(raw_numbers, list) else []:

   231	            continue

   233	            facts.append(NumberFact(**number))
   234	        except Exception:  # noqa: BLE001, S112 - a malformed number is dropped, not fatal

  1381	    reads the level to match a change column printed in basis points while the
  1382	    metric is points. NAB's FY25 ROE run read the RIGHT row — "Cash return on
  1383	    equity 11.4% 11.6% (20 bps)" — and then submitted 1160.0 -> 1140.0 ppt.
  1384	
  1385	    The correction is self-evidencing, exactly as the lift is: it fires only
  1386	    when the evidence PRINTS both endpoints, divided by 100, as percentages. A
  1387	    movement already written in points cannot pass that test, because no page
  1388	    prints an ROE of 0.116 per cent.
  1389	
  1390	    The gate is the METRIC's unit, which the taxonomy fixes, and never the
  1391	    movement's unit, which the model writes. Keyed on the model's label this
  1392	    corrector REVERSED the percent-to-bps lift: a CET1 movement the model had
